Name: Attractin/MKLN-like, beta-propeller domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the β-propeller domain (made up of Kelch repeats) found in attractin (ATRN), muskelin (MKLN), among others. ATRN is involved in the initial immune cell clustering during inflammatory response and may regulate chemotactic activity of chemokines. It may play a role in melanocortin signalling pathways that regulate energy homeostasis and hair colour [[cite:PUB00082152]]. It was thought to have dipeptidase activity but it was shown later to lack that activity [[cite:PUB00155414]]. Muskelin is a component of the CTLH E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex that selectively accepts ubiquitin from UBE2H and mediates ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of the transcription factor HBP1 [[cite:PUB00094808]]. It also acts as a mediator of cell spreading and cytoskeletal responses to the extracellular matrix component THBS1 [[cite:PUB00159952]].

This domain can be found in a number of other proteins, such as KLH25, a substrate-specific adapter of a BCR (BTB-CUL3-RBX1) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex involved in various processes, such as translation homeostasis and lipid synthesis [[cite:PUB00139484], [cite:PUB00159953]].

Name: INO80/SWR1 chromatin remodeling helicase
ShortDescription: The INO80/SWR1 helicase family is involved in chromatin remodeling and DNA repair. Members of this family function as ATPase components of various complexes, such as the INO80 and SWR1 complexes, which are responsible for shifting nucleosomes and exchanging histone variants. These activities lead to transcriptional regulation of selected genes and are essential for processes including DNA replication, DNA damage response, and mitotic chromosome segregation. Some family members are also implicated in developmental processes and the regulation of gene expression through histone modification exchange, contributing to cellular differentiation and response to environmental signals.

Name: DBINO domain
ShortDescription: Proteins belonging to the SNF2 family of DNA dependent ATPases are important members of the chromatin remodelling complexes that are implicated in epigenetic control of gene expression. Members of the SNF2 family of proteins have been identified in organisms ranging from Escherichia coli to Homo sapiens (Human). All of them contain the conserved SNF2 domain, which is defined by the existence of seven motifs (I, Ia, and II-VI) with sequences similarity to those motifs found in DNA and RNA helicases (see [prositedoc:PDOC51192]). SNF2-like family members can be further subdivided into several subfamilies according to the presence of protein motifs outside of the ATPase region. The DBINO (DNA binding domain of INO80) domain is characteristic of the INO80 subfamily and is a DNA-binding domain [[cite:PUB00052592], [cite:PUB00062156]]. The DBINO domain is a 126 amino acid long peptide located near the N terminus, approximately 100 residues upstream of the SNF2 helicase domain. The presence of this domain in all the INO80 subfamily proteins from yeast to humans suggests its conserved function in evolution [[cite:PUB00052592], [cite:PUB00052593]].

Name: DNA helicase INO80, DEAQ-box helicase domain
ShortDescription:
Ino80 is evolutionarily conserved from yeast to human [[cite:PUB00062156]]. It is an ATPase subunit of the INO80 complex [[cite:PUB00052593]]. The Ino80 complex displays 3'-5' DNA helicase activity and is involved in transcription, DNA replication and repair, and chromatin remodelling [[cite:PUB00074372], [cite:PUB00061630], [cite:PUB00074373]]. INO80 removes histone H3-containing nucleosomes from associated chromatin, promotes CENP-ACnp1 chromatin assembly at the centromere in a redundant manner with another chromatin-remodeling factor Chd1Hrp1 [[cite:PUB00101637]]. INO80 mutants have severe defects in oxygen consumption and promiscuous cell division that is no longer coupled with metabolic status [[cite:PUB00101636]]. INO80 is a member of the DEAD-like helicase superfamily.

This domain contains the ATP-binding region of INO80 from fungi and animals.

Name: NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase
ShortDescription: This domain is found in proteins that utilise NAD as a cofactor and use nucleotide-sugar substrates for a variety of chemical reactions [[cite:PUB00000446]]. One of the best studied of these proteins is UDP-galactose 4-epimerase which catalyses the conversion of UDP-galactose to UDP-glucose during galactose metabolism [[cite:PUB00025849], [cite:PUB00024593]].

Name: NAD(P)-dependent dehydratase-like
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes enzymes that are primarily involved in various biosynthetic pathways, including the production of flavonoids [[cite:PUB00155175]], lignin [[cite:PUB00155176]], meroterpenoids [[cite:PUB00154531]], and other polyketide-derived compounds. Members of this family function as oxidoreductases, often utilising NAD(P)H as a cofactor to catalyse the reduction of ketones and aldehydes to secondary alcohols. They play crucial roles in plant defense mechanisms, the formation of pigments, and the regulation of plant hormone levels. Some family members are also involved in the detoxification of harmful compounds and the biosynthesis of steroidal hormones in animals [[cite:PUB00118947]].

Name: Virilizer, yeast
ShortDescription: This entry includes virilizer (VIR1), the yeast homologue of human virilizer (VIRMA) [[cite:PUB00154326]]. VIR1 is a component of the MIS complex, a complex that mediates N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation of meiotic mRNAs and is required for initiation of meiosis, progression through the meiotic divisions and sporulation. In the complex, it plays a scaffolding role, stabilising the other complex members [[cite:PUB00154326]].

Name: Uncharacterized membrane protein YGR016W, fungi
ShortDescription: YGR016W contains an all helical fold. It is present with 238 molecules/cell in log phase SD medium [[cite:PUB00042821]].

Name: Rsc1/Rsc2, bromodomain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the bromodomain of Rsc1 and Rsc2 from budding yeasts. Bromodomains are 110 amino acid long domains, that are found in many chromatin associated proteins. Bromodomains can interact specifically with acetylated lysine.

The chromatin structure remodeling (RSC) complex consists at least of fifteen subunits, one of them being either RSC1 or RSC2. Neither RSC1 nor RSC2 is essential for viability, suggesting that they have some redundant function [[cite:PUB00063455]].

RSC is involved in transcription regulation and nucleosome positioning [[cite:PUB00063133]]. It is responsible for the transfer of a histone octamer from a nucleosome core particle to naked DNA [[cite:PUB00063134]]. The reaction requires ATP and involves an activated RSC-nucleosome intermediate. The remodeling reaction also involves DNA translocation, DNA twist and conformational change. As a reconfigurer of centromeric and flanking nucleosomes, RSC complex is required both for proper kinetochore function in chromosome segregation and, via a PKC1-dependent signaling pathway, for organisation of the cellular cytoskeleton [[cite:PUB00063135], [cite:PUB00063136], [cite:PUB00063137]]. In addition to being essential for mitotic growth, the RSC complex is also required for sporulation [[cite:PUB00063456]].

Name: Bromodomain, conserved site
ShortDescription:
Bromodomains are found in a variety of mammalian, invertebrate and yeast DNA-binding proteins [[cite:PUB00004405]]. Bromodomains are highly conserved α-helical motifs that can specifically interact with acetylated lysine residues on histone tails [[cite:PUB00005462], [cite:PUB00097275]]. In some proteins, the classical bromodomain has diverged to such an extent that parts of the region are either missing or contain an insertion (e.g., mammalian protein HRX, Caenorhabditis elegans hypothetical protein ZK783.4, yeast protein YTA7). The bromodomain may occur as a single copy, or in duplicate.

This domain is present in proteins involved in a wide range of functions such as acetylating histones, remodelling chromatin, and recruiting other factors necessary for transcription, thus playing a critical role in the regulation of transcription [[cite:PUB00097276]].

Name: Chromatin structure-remodeling complex subunit RSC1/2, bromodomain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the second bromodomain of RSC1/2 specific to fungi. RSC1 and RSC2 are components of the RSC complex (remodeling the structure of chromatin), are essential for transcriptional control, and have a specific domain architecture including two bromodomains [[cite:PUB00118328], [cite:PUB00063456], [cite:PUB00063135], [cite:PUB00118329], [cite:PUB00118330]]. The RSC complex has also been linked to homologous recombination and nonhomologous end-joining repair of DNA double strand breaks. Bromodomains are 110 amino acid long domains, that are found in many chromatin associated proteins. Bromodomains can interact specifically with acetylated lysine.

Name: Remodelling complex subunit Rsc/polybromo
ShortDescription:
There are two forms of the RSC remodelling complex in yeast, differing only in whether they contain the Rsc1 or Rsc2 subunits [[cite:PUB00063455]]. Rsc1 and Rsc2 have similar structures including two bromodomains and a BAH (Bromo-adjacent homology) domain [[cite:PUB00063455]].

There is only a single orthologue of Rsc1/Rsc2 in human cells, a protein designated BAF180 (or Polybromo), which appears to be a fusion protein of Rsc1, Rsc2 and a third RSC protein, Rsc4. BAF180 contains six bromodomains, followed by two BAH domains and an HMG domain close to the C terminus [[cite:PUB00018491]]. BAF180 is a subunit of the PBAF (or SWI/SNF-B) remodelling complex, which affects the transcription of many genes [[cite:PUB00086839], [cite:PUB00086840]]. Many human cancers have mutations in the gene encoding BAF180 [[cite:PUB00086841], [cite:PUB00086842]].

Name: Ribosome biogenesis protein Slx9-like
ShortDescription:
Slx9 is required for pre-rRNA processing. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Slx9 is associated with the 90S pre-ribosome and 43S small ribosomal subunit precursor [[cite:PUB00067595]].

The early stages of ribosomes biogenesis includes processing of the 35S pre-ribosomal RNA transcript into the mature 18S, 5.8S, and 25S rRNA molecules. The 35S precursor contains external transcribed spacer elements (5' and 3'-ETS) at either end as well as internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) that separate the mature sequences [[cite:PUB00067595]]. Slx9 is implicated in the processing events that remove the ITS1 spacer sequences [[cite:PUB00067595]].

Name: RagC/D
ShortDescription: RagC and RagD are closely related Rag GTPases (ras-related GTP-binding protein C and D) that constitute a unique subgroup of the Ras superfamily [[cite:PUB00089588]], and are functional homologues ofSaccharomyces cerevisiaeGtr2. They form heterodimers with RagA or RagB [[cite:PUB00007995]], and similarly, Gtr2 dimerizes with Gtr1 in order to function. They play an essential role in regulating amino acid-induced target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1) kinase signaling [[cite:PUB00060388]], exocytic cargo sorting at endosomes, and epigenetic control of gene expression. In response to amino acids, the Rag GTPases guide the TORC1 complex to activate the platform containing Rheb proto-oncogene by driving the relocalization of mTORC1 from discrete locations in the cytoplasm to a late endosomal and/or lysosomal compartment that is Rheb-enriched and contains Rab-7 [[cite:PUB00060388]].

Name: Gtr1/RagA G protein
ShortDescription:
GTR1 was first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Baker's yeast) as a suppressor of a mutation in RCC1. RCC1 catalyzes guanine nucleotide exchange on Ran, a well characterised nuclear Ras-like small G protein that plays an essential role in the import and export of proteins and RNAs across the nuclear membrane through the nuclear pore complex. RCC1 is located inside the nucleus, bound to chromatin. The concentration of GTP within the cell is ~30 times higher than the concentration of GDP, thus resulting in the preferential production of the GTP form of Ran by RCC1 within the nucleus.

Gtr1p is located within both the cytoplasm and the nucleus and has been reported to play a role in cell growth. Biochemical analysis revealed that Gtr1 is in fact a G protein of the Ras family. The RagA/B proteins are the human homologues of Gtr1 and Rag A and Gtr1p belong to the sixth subfamily of the Ras-like small GTPase superfamily [[cite:PUB00007995]].

Name: GTP1/OBG, conserved site
ShortDescription: A widespread family of GTP-binding proteins has been recently characterised [[cite:PUB00000217], [cite:PUB00001824]]. The function of the proteins that belong to this family is not yet known. They are polypeptides of about 40 to 48kDa which contain the five small sequence elements characteristic of GTP-binding proteins [[cite:PUB00004087]]. As a signature pattern was selected the region that correspond to the ATP/GTP B motif (also called G-3 in GTP-binding proteins).

Name: TGS
ShortDescription:
The TGS domain (named for its presence ThrRS, GTPase, and SpoT) is present in a number of enzymes, for example, in threonyl-tRNA synthetase (ThrRS), a distinct family of GTPases (the OBG family), and guanosine-3',5'-bis(diphosphate) 3'-pyrophosphohydrolase (SpoT) [[cite:PUB00007363], [cite:PUB00094831]] and synthetase (RelA) which are involved in stringent response in bacteria. The TGS domain is also present at the N-terminal of the uridine kinase from the spirochaete Treponema pallidum [[cite:PUB00094832]] (but not any other organism, including the related spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi).

TGS is a small domain that consists of ~50 amino acid residues and has nucleic acid binding affinity. It is arranged in a six-stranded half-barrel that curves around an α-helix and belongs to the β-grasp fold superfamily [[cite:PUB00016351], [cite:PUB00036769], [cite:PUB00034476]]. The function of the TGS domain of SpoT is in transcription of survival and virulence genes in response to environmental stress [[cite:PUB00095793]].

Name: Developmentally regulated GTP-binding protein
ShortDescription: Developmentally regulated G-proteins (DRGs) are a highly conserved family of GTP-binding proteins found in archaea, plants, fungi and animals, indicating important roles in fundamental pathways. DRG is a member of the Obg family, an evolutionary branch of GTPase superfamily proteins. GTPases act as molecular switches regulating diverse cellular processes. DRG2 and DRG1 comprise the DRG subfamily in eukaryotes. It has been proposed that the DRG subfamily proteins play their physiological roles through RNA binding [[cite:PUB00074840]].

Name: GTP binding protein, second domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain located C-terminal to [interpro:IPR006073] in a group of GTP binding proteins. In Ribosome-interacting GTPase 1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Rgb1) this entry represents a region of the G domain that contains the G3 and G4 motifs and folds as an independent domain emerging from the G domain, with an α/β configuration. It is essential for the full activity of the proteiin [[cite:PUB00076290]].

Name: Beta-grasp domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents a domain with a β-grasp fold and a core structure consisting of β(2)-α-β(2), which is similar to that found in ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00034476]]. Domains with this type of structure are found in the 2Fe-2S ferredoxin family (including putidaredoxin and adrenodoxin) [[cite:PUB00016348]], the 2Fe-2S ferredoxin-related family (including aldehyde reductase and xanthine dehydrogenase) [[cite:PUB00022831]], the TGS family (including threonyl-tRNA synthetase) [[cite:PUB00006444]] and the MoaD/ThiS family (including molybdopterin and thiamine biosynthesis sulphur carrier protein) [[cite:PUB00034477]].

Name: TGS-like
ShortDescription: The TGS domain is present in a number of enzymes, for example, in threonyl-tRNA synthetase (ThrRS), GTPase, and guanosine 3',5'-bis(diphosphate) 3'-pyrophosphohydrolase (SpoT) [[cite:PUB00007363]]. The TGS domain is also present at the amino terminus of the uridine kinase from the spirochaete Treponema pallidum (but not any other organism, including the related spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi).

Name: SDA1, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry includes SDA1 and its homologues. SDA1 is a Saccharomyces cerevisiae protein which is involved in the control of the actin cytoskeleton, essential for cell viability [[cite:PUB00016366], [cite:PUB00063830]]. It is a HEAT repeat-containing protein [[cite:PUB00101820]], required for 60S pre-ribosomal subunits export to the cytoplasm and may also be required for 60S ribosomal subunit maturation and accumulation [[cite:PUB00010459], [cite:PUB00063829]]. This entry represents the C-terminal region of SDA1 proteins.

Name: SDA1, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of SDA1 (also referred to as NUC130/133) [[cite:PUB00016366]]. It consists of HEAT repeats [[cite:PUB00101820]].

;

Sda1 is required for 60S pre-ribosomal subunits export to the cytoplasm and may also be required for 60S ribosomal subunit maturation and accumulation. It is involved in G1 events and passage through start, and possibly actin cytoskeleton organisation [[cite:PUB00010459], [cite:PUB00063829], [cite:PUB00063830]].

Name: SDA1, middle domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in several SDA1 protein homologues. SDA1 is a Saccharomyces cerevisiae protein which is involved in the control of the actin cytoskeleton. The protein is essential for cell viability and is localised in the nucleus [[cite:PUB00010459]].

Name: Sda1
ShortDescription: Sda1 is required for 60S pre-ribosomal subunits export to the cytoplasm and may also be required for 60S ribosomal subunit maturation and accumulation. It is involved in G1 events and passage through start, and possibly actin cytoskeleton organisation [[cite:PUB00010459], [cite:PUB00063829], [cite:PUB00063830]].

Name: mRNA decapping protein 2, Box A domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents the box A specific to mRNA decapping protein 2 [swissprot:P53550], Dcp2, the catalytic subunit of the mRNA-decapping enzyme [[cite:PUB00010148]], which is found at the N-terminal of the NUDIX hydrolase domain [interpro:IPR000086]. Removal of the cap structure is mediated by the Dcp1-Dcp2 complex [[cite:PUB00033653]].

The Box A domain contains a four helices fold and an orthogonal array of two α-hairpins topology.

Name: mRNA decapping enzyme 2 , NUDIX hydrolase domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the NUDIX hydrolase domain found in Dcp2. This domain catalyses the mRNA decapping reaction [[cite:PUB00094963]].

;

Dcp2 is the catalytic component of the decapping complex necessary for the degradation of mRNAs, both in normal mRNA turnover and in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay [[cite:PUB00094961], [cite:PUB00094962]]. Dcp2 contains an all-α N-terminal helical domain and a domain which has the Nudix fold. It has been shown that the Nudix domain of both Saccharomyces cerevisiae and S. pombe Dcp2 proteins is sufficient for decapping activity. While decapping is not dependent on the N-terminal of Dcp2, it does affect its efficiency. Dcp1 binds the N-terminal domain of Dcp2 stimulating the decapping activity of Dcp2 [[cite:PUB00033653]].

Name: mRNA decapping protein 2, Box A domain
ShortDescription: This presumed domain is always found to the N-terminal side of the NUDIX hydrolase domain [interpro:IPR000086]. This domain appears to be specific to mRNA decapping protein 2 (DCP2) [swissprot:P53550] and its close homologues. This region has been termed Box A [[cite:PUB00010148]].

Name: Carbohydrate kinase FGGY, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the C-terminal domain of these proteins. It adopts a ribonuclease H-like fold and is structurally related to the N-terminal domain [[cite:PUB00005161], [cite:PUB00019551]].

;

FGGY carbohydrate kinases carry out ATP-dependent phosphorylation on one out of at least nine distinct sugar substrates [[cite:PUB00080793]]. These enzymes include L-ribulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.16]) (gene araB); Erythriol kinase ([ec:2.7.1.27]) (gene eryA); L-fucolokinase ([ec:2.7.1.51]) (gene fucK); gluconokinase ([ec:2.7.1.12]) (gene gntK); glycerol kinase ([ec:2.7.1.30]) (gene glpK); xylulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.17]) (gene xylB); L-xylulose kinase ([ec:2.7.1.53]) (gene lyxK), D-ribulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.47]) (gene rbtK); and rhamnulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.5]) (gene rhaB). This family also contains a divergent subfamily functioning in quorum sensing, which phosphorylates AI-2, a bacterial signaling molecule derived from 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD) [[cite:PUB00056209]].

;

All described members of this enzyme family are composed of two homologous actin-like ATPase domains. A catalytic cleft is formed by the interface between these two domains, where the sugar substrate and ATP co-substrate bind.

Name: Carbohydrate kinase FGGY, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of these proteins. It adopts a ribonuclease H-like fold and is structurally related to the C-terminal domain [[cite:PUB00005161], [cite:PUB00019551]].

;

FGGY carbohydrate kinases carry out ATP-dependent phosphorylation on one out of at least nine distinct sugar substrates [[cite:PUB00080793]]. These enzymes include L-ribulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.16]) (gene araB); Erythriol kinase ([ec:2.7.1.27]) (gene eryA); L-fucolokinase ([ec:2.7.1.51]) (gene fucK); gluconokinase ([ec:2.7.1.12]) (gene gntK); glycerol kinase ([ec:2.7.1.30]) (gene glpK); xylulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.17]) (gene xylB); L-xylulose kinase ([ec:2.7.1.53]) (gene lyxK), D-ribulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.47]) (gene rbtK); and rhamnulokinase ([ec:2.7.1.5]) (gene rhaB). This family also contains a divergent subfamily functioning in quorum sensing, which phosphorylates AI-2, a bacterial signaling molecule derived from 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD) [[cite:PUB00056209]].

Name: CobW-like, C-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
CobW proteins are generally found proximal to the trimeric cobaltochelatase subunit CobN, which is essential for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00015657], [cite:PUB00078797]]. They contain a P-loop nucleotide-binding loop in the N-terminal domain and a histidine-rich region in the C-terminal portion suggesting a role in metal binding, possibly as an intermediary between the cobalt transport and chelation systems. CobW might be involved in cobalt reduction leading to cobalt(I) corrinoids.

This entry represents the C-terminal domain found in CobW, as well as in P47K ([swissprot:P31521]), a Pseudomonas chlororaphis protein needed for nitrile hydratase expression [[cite:PUB00035321]].

Name: CobW/HypB/UreG, nucleotide-binding domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found in HypB, a hydrogenase expression/formation protein, and urease accessory protein UreG. Both these proteins contain a P-loop nucleotide binding motif [[cite:PUB00002310], [cite:PUB00002230]]. HypB has GTPase activity and is a guanine nucleotide binding protein [[cite:PUB00002230]]. UreG is a GTPase in charge of nucleotide hydrolysis required for activation of the urease enzyme [[cite:PUB00078798]]. Both GTPases are involved in nickel binding. HypB can store nickel and is required for nickel dependent hydrogenase expression [[cite:PUB00003878]]. UreG is required for functional incorporation of the urease nickel metallocentre [[cite:PUB00002187]]. GTP hydrolysis may required by these proteins for nickel incorporation into other nickel proteins [[cite:PUB00003878]].

Other proteins containing this domain include P47K ([swissprot:P31521]), a Pseudomonas chlororaphis protein needed for nitrile hydratase expression, CobW ([swissprot:P29937]), which may be involved in cobalamin biosynthesis in Pseudomonas denitrificans [[cite:PUB00008140]], and YjiA [[cite:PUB00029084]]. Both CobW and YjiA are members of the metal homeostasis-associated COG0523 family of GTPases [[cite:PUB00078797]].

Name: Zinc-regulated GTPase metalloprotein activator
ShortDescription: This family of proteins functions as zinc chaperones, facilitating the transfer of zinc ions to target metalloproteins, which results in their activation. The proteins possess a GTPase domain with a CXCC motif that binds zinc and, upon GTP hydrolysis, transfers the zinc to specific binding sites on metalloproteins. This process is essential for the proper function of metalloenzymes such as methionine aminopeptidase METAP1, which cleaves initiator methionine from nascent polypeptides. The activity of these GTPases is regulated by metal binding; zinc inhibits while other metals like Co(II) and Ni(II) decrease the GTPase activity. These proteins are part of the SIMIBI class G3E GTPase family within the ZNG1 subfamily.

Name: Zinc chaperone CobW-like, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
CobW proteins are generally found proximal to the trimeric cobaltochelatase subunit CobN, which is essential for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00015657], [cite:PUB00078797]]. They contain a P-loop nucleotide-binding loop in the N-terminal domain and a histidine-rich region in the C-terminal portion suggesting a role in metal binding, possibly as an intermediary between the cobalt transport and chelation systems. CobW might be involved in cobalt reduction leading to cobalt(I) corrinoids.

This entry represents the C-terminal domain found in CobW, as well as in P47K ([swissprot:P31521]), a Pseudomonas chlororaphis protein needed for nitrile hydratase expression [[cite:PUB00035321]].

;

Cobalamin (vitamin B12) is a structurally complex cofactor, consisting of a modified tetrapyrrole with a centrally chelated cobalt. Cobalamin is usually found in one of two biologically active forms: methylcobalamin and adocobalamin. Most prokaryotes, as well as animals, have cobalamin-dependent enzymes, whereas plants and fungi do not appear to use it. In bacteria and archaea, these include methionine synthase, ribonucleotide reductase, glutamate and methylmalonyl-CoA mutases, ethanolamine ammonia lyase, and diol dehydratase [[cite:PUB00015657]]. In mammals, cobalamin is obtained through the diet, and is required for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase [[cite:PUB00035308]].

Name: Nucleolar GTP-binding protein 2, circularly permuted GTPase motif
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the circularly permuted GTPase motif of Nucleolar GTP-binding protein 2 (GNL2, also known as NGP-1) from animals and fungi. GNL2 is a GTPase that associates with pre-60S ribosomal subunits in the nucleolus and is required for their nuclear export and maturation [[cite:PUB00101554]].

This group of proteins also includes Nuclear/nucleolar GTPase 2 (NUG2) from plants [[cite:PUB00072522]].

Name: Nucleolar GTP-binding protein 2, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This N-terminal domain is found in Nucleolar GTP-binding protein 2 [[cite:PUB00056824]].

Name: CCR4-NOT transcription complex subunit 9
ShortDescription: This entry includes CCR4-NOT transcription complex subunit 9 (CNOT9 or Rcd1). Mammalian CNOT9 is a component of the CCR4-NOT complex which is one of the major cellular mRNA deadenylases and is linked to various cellular processes including bulk mRNA degradation, miRNA-mediated repression, translational repression during translational initiation and general transcription regulation [[cite:PUB00075516]].

Name: Vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein IST1-like
ShortDescription: The endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) machinery functions in several important eukaryotic cellular processes such as MVB (multivesicular body) formation. The AAA-ATPase Vps4 catalyzes disassembly of the ESCRT-III complex and may regulate membrane deformation and vesicle scission as well. Ist1 acts as a negative regulator of the MVB pathway by binding to the N-terminal MIT (microtubule interacting and transport) domain of Vps4 through its C-terminal region, with its 15 amino acids bearing strong homology to a conserved sequence motif called MIM1 (MIT interacting motif 1 [[cite:PUB00052965]]). This MIT domain is found in various proteins and enzymes including ubiquitin hydrolases proteases, ATPases (Spastin and VPS4 proteins) and ATPase activators (Vta1p/LIP5) [[cite:PUB00052035]].

Name: Vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein Ist1
ShortDescription: Budding yeast Ist1 is involved in a late step in sorting of cargo proteins of the multivesicular body (MVB) for incorporation into intralumenal vesicles [[cite:PUB00077601]]. This entry also includes Ist1 homologues from animals and plants. Human Ist1 functions in the ESCRT (endosomal sorting complexes required for transport) pathway and is required for efficient abscission during HeLa cell cytokinesis [[cite:PUB00077602]]. Human Ist1 binds the transport (MIT) domain of VPS4, LIP5, and Spartin via its C-terminal MIT-interacting motif (MIM) [[cite:PUB00077607]].

Name: Multifunctional chaperone and stress response protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes co-chaperones that may interact with HSP70 and are implicated in ribosomal RNA biogenesis, particularly in the maturation of the 60S ribosomal subunit. Some members are involved in chromatin-related processes, such as position-effect variegation and chromosome condensation. Others function in cellular stress responses, including ER-phagy during ER stress, and in regulatory pathways affecting drug resistance. Common motifs such as the atg8-interaction motif and the FFAT motif suggest roles in protein-protein interactions, essential for their diverse functions.

Name: Zinc finger, double-stranded RNA binding
ShortDescription: This zinc finger is mainly found in eukaryotic sequences, and is approximately 30 amino acids in length. The mammalian members of this group occur multiple times along the protein, joined by flexible linkers, and are referred to as JAZ - dsRNA-binding ZF protein - zinc-fingers. The JAZ proteins are expressed in all tissues tested and localise in the nucleus, particularly the nucleolus [[cite:PUB00053807]]. JAZ preferentially binds to double-stranded (ds) RNA or RNA/DNA hybrids rather than DNA. In addition to binding double-stranded RNA, these zinc-fingers are required for nucleolar localisation.

Name: Zuotin-like, zuotin homology domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in Zuotin from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ZUO1) and in similar eukaryotic sequences. ZUO1 is a component of the ribosome-associated complex (RAC), a heterodimeric chaperone complex involved in the regulation of accurate translation termination and in folding or maintaining nascent polypeptides in a folding-competent state. This entry represents its zuotin homology domain (ZHD), which is functionally important for association with ribosomes. It folds into four helices, including a three helix bundle [[cite:PUB00096580]]. It is normally found C-terminal to the DnaJ domain ([interpro:IPR001623]).

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL22
ShortDescription:
Large ribosomal subunit protein uL22 (also known as L22 in bacteria and previously known as L17 in eukaryotes) is a core protein of the large ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00080279]]. It is the only ribosomal protein that interacts with all six domains of 23S rRNA, and is one of the proteins important for directing the proper folding and stabilizing the conformation of 23S rRNA. uL22 is the largest protein contributor to the surface of the polypeptide exit channel, the tunnel through which the polypeptide product passes. uL22 is also one of six proteins located at the putative translocon binding site on the exterior surface of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00028498], [cite:PUB00025895]].

;

Ribosomes are the particles that catalyse mRNA-directed protein synthesis in all organisms. The codons of the mRNA are exposed on the ribosome to allow tRNA binding. This leads to the incorporation of amino acids into the growing polypeptide chain in accordance with the genetic information. Incoming amino acid monomers enter the ribosomal A site in the form of aminoacyl-tRNAs complexed with elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and GTP. The growing polypeptide chain, situated in the P site as peptidyl-tRNA, is then transferred to aminoacyl-tRNA, and the new peptidyl-tRNA, extended by one residue, is translocated to the P site with the aid of the elongation factor G (EF-G) and GTP as the deacylated tRNA is released from the ribosome through one or more exit sites [[cite:PUB00007068], [cite:PUB00007069]]. About 2/3 of the mass of the ribosome consists of RNA and 1/3 consists of protein. The proteins are named in accordance with the subunit of the ribosome which they belong to: the small (S1 to S31) and the large (L1 to L44). Usually they decorate the rRNA cores of the subunits.

Many ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large subunit, are composed of a globular, surfaced-exposed domain with long finger-like projections that extend into the rRNA core to stabilise its structure. Most of the proteins interact with multiple RNA elements, often from different domains. In the large subunit, about 1/3 of the 23S rRNA nucleotides are at least in van der Waals' contact with protein, and L22 interacts with all six domains of the 23S rRNA. Proteins S4 and S7, which initiate assembly of the 16S rRNA, are located at junctions of five and four RNA helices, respectively. In this way, proteins serve to organise and stabilise the rRNA tertiary structure. While the crucial activities of decoding and peptide transfer are RNA-based, proteins play an active role in functions that may have evolved to streamline the process of protein synthesis. In addition to their function in the ribosome, many ribosomal proteins have some function 'outside' the ribosome [[cite:PUB00007069], [cite:PUB00007070]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL22, bacteria/organella
ShortDescription:
This entry represents large ribosomal subunit protein uL22 found in bacteria and eukaryotic organelles such as chloroplast and mitochondria.

Name: Ribosomal protein uL22 superfamily
ShortDescription: Large ribosomal subunit protein uL22 (also known as L22 in bacteria and previously known as L17 in eukaryotes) is a core protein of the large ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00080279]]. It is the only ribosomal protein that interacts with all six domains of 23S rRNA, and is one of the proteins important for directing the proper folding and stabilizing the conformation of 23S rRNA. uL22 is the largest protein contributor to the surface of the polypeptide exit channel, the tunnel through which the polypeptide product passes. uL22 is also one of six proteins located at the putative translocon binding site on the exterior surface of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00028498], [cite:PUB00025895]].

Name: Nop13/Rnp24, RNA recognition motif 2
ShortDescription: This entry represents the RNA recognition motif 2 (RR2) of Nop13p from Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It shares high sequence similarity with nucleolar protein 12 (Nop12p). Neither Nop12p nor Nop13p are essential for growth. However, unlike Nop12p that is localized to the nucleolus, Nop13p localizes primarily to the nucleolus but is also present in the nucleoplasm to a lesser extent. Nop13p contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) [[cite:PUB00045310]]. Proteins containing this domain include Rnp24 from S. pombe.

Name: Nop13/Rnp24, RNA recognition motif 1
ShortDescription: This entry represents the RNA recognition motif 1 (RRM1) of Nop13p from Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It shares high sequence similarity with nucleolar protein 12 (Nop12p). Neither Nop12p nor Nop13p are essential for growth. However, unlike Nop12p that is localized to the nucleolus, Nop13p localizes primarily to the nucleolus but is also present in the nucleoplasm to a lesser extent. Nop13p contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) [[cite:PUB00045310]]. Proteins containing this domain include Rnp24 from S. pombe.

Name: Rho-associated Serine/Threonine Kinase
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes serine/threonine kinases that are key regulators of the actin cytoskeleton and cell polarity. They are involved in various cellular processes such as smooth muscle contraction, cytoskeleton organization, stress fiber and focal adhesion formation, cell adhesion and motility, cytokinesis, and cell migration. Members of this family play roles in the phosphorylation of a range of substrates leading to the regulation of actomyosin contractility, cell protrusion, and migration. They are also implicated in the regulation of centrosome duplication, angiogenesis, and various differentiation processes including keratinocyte terminal differentiation and erythroid differentiation. Activation of these kinases is typically regulated by RHOA binding and can be inhibited by specific compounds. Some members are involved in the regulation of synaptic properties and circadian rhythms in vascular contractility.

Name: Prefoldin, subunit 4
ShortDescription: This group represents a prefoldin, subunit 4 (PFDN4, also known as Gim3 in budding yeasts). PFDN4 is part of the prefoldin heterohexamer copmlex (consists of two PFD-alpha type and four PFD-beta type subunits) that binds specifically to cytosolic chaperonin (c-CPN) and transfers targeted proteins to it. It binds to nascent polypeptide chain and promotes folding in an environment in which there are many competing pathways for nonnative proteins [[cite:PUB00008051], [cite:PUB00063296]].

Name: TmcA/NAT10, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found at the N-terminal of TmcA from bacteria and NAT10 from eukaryotes.

;

The bacterial tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase (TmcA) catalyses the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine (ac4C) at the wobble position of tRNA(Met), by using acetyl-CoA as an acetyl donor and either ATP or GTP [[cite:PUB00056806]]. This modification is thought to ensure precise recognition of the AUG codon by strengthening C-G base-pair interaction and also prevent misrecognition of the near cognate AUA codon [[cite:PUB00050413]]. RNA cytidine acetyltransferas (NAT10) are RNA cytosine acetyltransferases with specificity toward both 18S rRNA and tRNAs and contain additional putative nuclear and nucleolar localisation signals (NLS and NoLS respectively) [[cite:PUB00076725], [cite:PUB00076726], [cite:PUB00107449]].

Name: RNA cytidine acetyltransferase NAT10
ShortDescription:
RNA cytidine acetyltransferase NAT10 has specificity toward both 18S rRNA and tRNAs and catalyzes the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine at two positions in 18S rRNA. NAT10 is required for early nucleolar cleavages of precursor rRNA at sites A0, A1 and A2 during 18S rRNA synthesis [[cite:PUB00077545], [cite:PUB00076725]]. NAT10 also catalyzes the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine at a single position in serine and leucine tRNAs. The tRNA-binding adapter protein TAN1 is required for full tRNA acetyltransferase activity but not for 18S rRNA acetylation [[cite:PUB00076725]].

Human NAT10 is a lysine acetyltransferase that targets microtubules and histones, and plays an important role in cell division. It is highly expressed in malignant tumors [[cite:PUB00080263]].

Name: Possible tRNA binding domain
ShortDescription: This domain, found at the C terminus of tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase, may be involved in tRNA-binding [[cite:PUB00050413]]. tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA catalyses the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine (ac4C) at the wobble position of tRNA(Met), by using acetyl-CoA as an acetyl donor and ATP (or GTP) [[cite:PUB00056806]].

ShortDescription:
This entry includes bacterial tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA and eukaryotic N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10). They consist of an RNA helicase domain and a GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) domain.

Name: TcmA/NAT10, helicase domain
ShortDescription:
This domain contains a P-loop (Walker A) motif, suggesting that it has ATPase activity, and a Walker B motif. It is found in NAT10 from eukaryotes and TmcA from prokaryotes. In NAT10, this domain catalyses the formation of N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification on mRNAs, 18S rRNA and tRNAs [[cite:PUB00076725], [cite:PUB00158942], [cite:PUB00158943]]. In TmcA, it may function as an RNA helicase motor (driven by ATP hydrolysis) which delivers the wobble base to the active centre of the GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) domain [[cite:PUB00050413]].

Name: Ribosome biogenesis protein 15, RNA recognition motif
ShortDescription: This entry represents the RNA recognition motif (RRM) of Nop15. Nop15 has been identified as a component of a pre-60S particle. It interacts with RNA components of the early pre-60S particles. Furthermore, Nop15 binds directly to a pre-rRNA transcript in vitro and is required for pre-rRNA processing. It functions as a ribosome synthesis factor required for the 5' to 3' exonuclease digestion that generates the 5' end of the major, short form of the 5.8S rRNA as well as for processing of 27SB to 7S pre-rRNA. Nop15p also play a specific role in cell cycle progression [[cite:PUB00083590]]. Nop15p contains an RNA recognition motif (RRM).

Name: Atypical dual-specificity phosphatase Siw14-like
ShortDescription: This group of atypical dual-specificity phosphatases are predominantly from fungi, plants and bacteria. This entry includes budding yeast Siw14 (also known as Oca3) and related proteins. Siw14 is a inositol pyrophosphate phosphatase that modulates inositol pyrophosphate metabolism by dephosphorylating the IP7 isoform 5PP-IP5to IP6 [[cite:PUB00088170]]. This entry also includes budding yeast Oca1/2/4/6 and Arabidopsis DSP1/2/3/4/5. All DSPs tested (AtPFA-DSP1, -2, -3, and -5) displayed phosphatase activity toward PI(3,5)P2, with AtPFA-DSP2 showing a higher activity [[cite:PUB00088172]]. Oca1/2/4/6 are putative phosphatases associated with the caffeine-sensitivity stress pathway in S. cerevisiae [[cite:PUB00088172]]. It also includes dual specificity protein phosphatase TpbA that regulates diverse phenotypes in P.aeruginosa via regulation of the concentration of cellular c-di-GMP [[cite:PUB00078743]]. This phosphatase acts by dephosphorylating the membrane-anchored diguanylate cyclase TpbB at tyrosine and serine/threonine sites, leading to inactivation of TpbB and reduced c-di-GMP production [[cite:PUB00078743], [cite:PUB00151104]].

Name: Atypical dual-specificity phosphatase Siw14-like, plant and fungi
ShortDescription: This entry represent a group of atypical dual-specificity phosphatases from plant and fungi. Proteins in this entry include Siw14 and related proteins [[cite:PUB00088172]]. Siw14 is a inositol pyrophosphate phosphatase that modulates inositol pyrophosphate metabolism by dephosphorylating the IP7isoform 5PP-IP5to IP6 [[cite:PUB00088170]]. This entry also includes DSP1/2/3/4/5 from Arabidopsis. All DSPs tested (AtPFA-DSP1, -2, -3, and -5) displayed phosphatase activity toward PI(3,5)P2, with AtPFA-DSP2 showing a higher activity [[cite:PUB00088172]].

Name: DNA/RNA polymerase superfamily
ShortDescription: This entry represents the DNA/RNA polymerase superfamily, which includes DNA polymerase I, reverse transcriptase, T7 RNA polymerase, lesion bypass DNA polymerase (Y-family), RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase and dsRNA phage RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase. These enzymes share a similar protein fold at their active site, which resembles the palm subdomain of the right-hand-shaped polymerases [[cite:PUB00094074]].

Name: DNA-directed DNA-polymerase, family A, mitochondria
ShortDescription:
DNA carries the biological information that instructs cells how to exist in an ordered fashion. Accurate replication is thus one of the most important events in the cell life cycle. This function is mediated by DNA-directed DNA-polymerases, which add nucleotide triphosphate (dNTP) residues to the 5'-end of the growing DNA chain, using a complementary DNA as template. Small RNA molecules are generally used as primers for chain elongation, although terminal proteins may also be used.

DNA-dependent DNA-polymerases have been grouped into families, denoted A, B and X, on the basis of sequence similarities [[cite:PUB00004647], [cite:PUB00004955]]. Members of family A, which includes bacterial and bacteriophage polymerases, share significant similarity to Escherichia coli polymerase I; hence family A is also known as the pol I family. The bacterial polymerases also contain an exonuclease activity, which is coded for in the N-terminal portion. The yeast gamma polymerases show some similarity to the prokaryotic nuclear polymerases of family A, but their function is restricted to mitochondrial DNA replication and repair [[cite:PUB00002437]].

Name: DNA mitochondrial polymerase, exonuclease domain
ShortDescription: This domain belongs to human mitochondrial DNA polymerase (Pol-gamma). Pol-gamma has a catalytic subunit, Pol gamma-A, which possesses both polymerase and proofreading exonuclease activities and an accessory subunit, Pol gamma-B, which accelerates polymerization rate and suppresses exonuclease activity. This domain is the exonuclease domain of the catalytic subunit, Pol gamma-A [[cite:PUB00054802]].

Name: DNA-directed DNA polymerase, family A, palm domain
ShortDescription:
Synonym(s): DNA nucleotidyltransferase (DNA-directed)

DNA-directed DNA polymerases([ec:2.7.7.7]) are the key enzymes catalysing the accurate replication of DNA. They require either a small RNA molecule or a protein as a primer for thede novosynthesis of a DNA chain. A number of polymerases belong to this family [[cite:PUB00004955], [cite:PUB00004393], [cite:PUB00004443]].

;

DNA-dependent DNA polymerases can be classified into six main groups based upon phylogenetic relationships with E. coli polymerase I (classA), E. coli polymerase II (class B), E.coli polymerase III (class C), euryarchaeota polymerase II (class D), human polymerase beta (class X), E. coli UmuC/DinB and eukaryotic RAP 30/Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (class Y). The structure of these polymerases resembles in overall morphology a cupped human right hand, with fingers (which bind an incoming nucleotide and interact with the single-stranded template), palm (which harbors the catalytic amino acid residues and also binds an incoming dNTP) and thumb (which binds double-stranded DNA) subdomains [[cite:PUB00092104]].

Name: DNA-directed DNA polymerase, family A, conserved site
ShortDescription:
DNA carries the biological information that instructs cells how to exist in an ordered fashion: accurate replication is thus one of the most important events in the cell life cycle. This function is mediated by DNA-directed DNA-polymerases, which add nucleotide triphosphate (dNTP) residues to the 3'-end of the growing DNA chain, using a complementary DNA as template. Small RNA molecules are generally used as primers for chain elongation, although terminal proteins may also be used. Three motifs, A, B and C [[cite:PUB00004955]], are seen to be conserved across all DNA-polymerases, with motifs A and C also seen in RNA- polymerases. They are centred on invariant residues, and their structural significance was implied from the Klenow (Escherichia coli) structure: motif A contains a strictly-conserved aspartate at the junction of a β-strand and an α-helix; motif B contains an α-helix with positive charges; and motif C has a doublet of negative charges, located in a β-turn-β secondary structure [[cite:PUB00004955]].

DNA polymerases ([ec:2.7.7.7]) can be classified, on the basis of sequence similarity [[cite:PUB00004647], [cite:PUB00004955]], into at least four different groups: A, B, C and X. Members of family X are small (about 40kDa) compared with other polymerases and encompass two distinct polymerase enzymes that have similar functionality: vertebrate polymerase beta (same as yeast pol 4), and terminal deoxynucleotidyl-transferase (TdT) ([ec:2.7.7.31]). The former functions in DNA repair, while the latter terminally adds single nucleotides to polydeoxynucleotide chains. Both enzymes catalyse addition of nucleotides in a distributive manner, i.e. they dissociate from the template-primer after addition of each nucleotide. DNA-polymerases show a degree of structural similarity with RNA-polymerases.

;

Five regions of similarity are found in all the polymerases of this entry. The signature of this entry is to the conserved region, known as 'motif B' [[cite:PUB00004955]]; motif B is located in a domain which, in E. coli polA, has been shown to bind deoxynucleotide triphosphate substrates; it contains a conserved tyrosine which has been shown, by photo-affinity labelling, to be in the active site; a conserved lysine, also part of this motif, can be chemically labelled, using pyridoxal phosphate.

Name: DNA polymerase gamma, palm domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the palm domain of human DNA polymerase gammaA (Pol gammaA), the catalytic subunit of the mitochondrial DNA polymerase, and similar proteins from animals and fungi. This subunit possesses both polymerase and proofreading exonuclease activities, and together with the accessory subunit, Pol gammaB, constitute the Pol gamma holoenzyme. This protein is important for mitochondrial DNA maintenance and mutation of the catalytic subunit of Pol gamma is implicated in more than 30 human diseases. The holoenzyme is a heterotrimer containing one Pol gammaA subunit and a dimeric Pol gammaB subunit. The Pol gammaA belongs to classA polymerases and its palm domain adopts a canonical polymerase configuration [pdbe:3IKM] [[cite:PUB00054802], [cite:PUB00022118], [cite:PUB00103822], [cite:PUB00103821]].

Name: ClpP/crotonase-like domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents a ClpP/crotonase-like domain formed from repeated β/β/α units, which comprises two perpendicular β-sheet surrounded by α-helices. Proteins containing this domain can be classified into four structural families [[cite:PUB00069782]]:

  • The Clp protease, Clp subunit family.
  • The tail-specific protease, catalytic domain family. Members include tricorn proteases.
  • The crotonase-like family.
  • The biotin-dependent carboxylase carboxyltransferase domain family. Members include the acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase carboxyl transferase subunits.

Name: ClpP, Ser active site
ShortDescription:
Clp is an ATP-dependent protease that cleaves a number of proteins, such as casein and albumin [[cite:PUB00002564]]. It exists as a heterodimer of ATP-binding regulatory A and catalytic P subunits, both of which are required for effective levels of protease activity in the presence of ATP [[cite:PUB00002564]], although the P subunit alone does possess some catalytic activity.

Proteases highly similar to ClpP have been found to be encoded in the genome of bacteria, metazoa, some viruses and in the chloroplast of plants. A number of the proteins in this family are classified as non-peptidase homologues as they have been found experimentally to be without peptidase activity, or lack amino acid residues that are believed to be essential for catalytic activity.

ShortDescription:

Name: ATP-dependent Clp protease proteolytic subunit
ShortDescription:
Clp is an ATP-dependent protease that cleaves a number of proteins, such as casein and albumin [[cite:PUB00002564]] and is a member of peptidase family S14. It exists as a heterodimer of ATP-binding regulatory A and catalytic P subunits, both of which are required for effective levels of protease activity in the presence of ATP [[cite:PUB00002564], [cite:PUB00081432]], although the P subunit alone does possess some catalytic activity [[cite:PUB00085963]]. This entry represents the P subunit.

Proteases highly similar to ClpP have been found to be encoded in the genome of bacteria, metazoa, some viruses and in the chloroplast of plants, but seems to be absent in archaea, mollicutes and some fungi [[cite:PUB00081435]].

Name: ClpP, histidine active site
ShortDescription:
The endopeptidase Clp ([ec:3.4.21.92]) from Escherichia coli cleaves peptides in various proteins in a process that requires ATP hydrolysis [[cite:PUB00002565], [cite:PUB00003609]]. Clp is a dimeric protein which consists of a proteolytic subunit (gene clpP) and either of two related ATP-binding regulatory subunits (genes clpA and clpX). ClpP is a serine protease which has a chymotrypsin-like activity. Its catalytic activity seems to be provided by a charge relay system similar to that of the trypsin family of serine proteases, but which evolved by independent convergent evolution.

Proteases highly similar to ClpP have been found to be encoded in the genome of the chloroplast of plants and seem to be also present in other eukaryotes.

This entry represents a conserved region containing a histidine that is involved in the catalytic triad.

Name: AAA lid domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the α-helical AAA+ lid domain that is found to the C terminus of AAA domains.

Name: Origin recognition complex subunit 1, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal winged helix-turn-helix domain found in fungal Origin recognition complex subunit 1 proteins [[cite:PUB00151759]].

Name: Origin recognition complex 1/Cell division control protein 6
ShortDescription: The ORC1/CDC6 family includes proteins that are key regulators of DNA replication. Members of the family are involved in the initiation of DNA replication by binding to origins of replication, which is often ATP-dependent. They play a role in the assembly of the pre-replication complex necessary to commence DNA replication. Some family members also participate in checkpoint controls to ensure DNA replication is completed before mitosis begins. Additionally, certain proteins within the family have roles in transcriptional silencing, chromatin structure modulation, and cell cycle control of replication. They may bind to specific DNA sequences, such as the ARS consensus sequence in some species, and can interact with other proteins like the MCM helicase complex to regulate the replication process.

Name: Transmembrane emp24 domain-containing protein
ShortDescription:
This group of proteins consists of TMP21 (also known as transmembrane emp24 domain-containing protein 10) and related proteins, which are members of the p24 family. The p24 family is a widely conserved family of transmembrane proteins that plays a functional role in the initiation of assembly of COPI (Coat protein I) coated vesicles. COPI coated vesicles are involved in protein transport within the early secretory pathway [[cite:PUB00034783], [cite:PUB00034784]].

p24 proteins are major membrane components of COPI- and COPII-coated vesicles and are implicated in cargo selectivity of ER to Golgi transport [[cite:PUB00003083], [cite:PUB00009426]]. Multiple members of the p24 family are found in all eukaryotes, from yeast to mammals. Members of the p24 family are type I membrane proteins with a signal peptide at the amino terminus, a lumenal coiled-coil (extracytosolic) domain, a single transmembrane domain with conserved amino acids, and a short cytoplasmic tail. They may be grouped into at least three subfamilies based on primary sequence [[cite:PUB00009427]]. One subfamily comprises yeast Emp24p and mammalian p24A. Another subfamily comprises yeast Erv25p and mammalian Tmp21, and the third subfamily comprises mammalian gp25L proteins.

Name: GOLD domain
ShortDescription:
The GOLD (for Golgi dynamics) domain is a protein module found in several eukaryotic Golgi and lipid-traffic proteins. It is typically between 90 and 150 amino acids long. Most of the size difference observed in the GOLD-domain superfamily is traceable to a single large low-complexity insert that is seen in some versions of the domain. With the exception of the p24 proteins, which have a simple architecture with the GOLD domain as their only globular domain, all other GOLD-domain proteins contain additional conserved globular domains. In these proteins, the GOLD domain co-occurs with lipid-, sterol-or fatty acid-binding domains such as PH, CRAL-TRIO, FYVE oxysterol binding-and acyl CoA-binding domains, suggesting that these proteins may interact with membranes. The GOLD domain can also be found associated with a RUN domain, which may have a role in the interaction of various proteins with cytoskeletal filaments. The GOLD domain is predicted to mediate diverse protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00011844]]. A secondary structure prediction for the GOLD domain reveals that it is likely to adopt a compact all-β-fold structure with six to seven strands. Most of the sequence conservation is centred on the hydrophobic cores that support these predicted strands. The predicted secondary-structure elements and the size of the conserved core of the domain suggests that it may form a β-sandwich fold with the strands arranged in two β-sheets stacked on each other [[cite:PUB00011844]].

Some proteins known to contain a GOLD domain are listed below:

  • Eukaryotic proteins of the p24 family.
  • Animal Sec14-like proteins. They are involved in secretion.
  • Human Golgi resident protein GCP60. It interacts with the Golgi integral membrane protein Giantin.
  • Yeast oxysterol-binding protein homologue 3 (OSH3).
  • Plant Patellin 1-6. It may be involved in membrane-trafficking events [[cite:PUB00160400]].

Name: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-coenzyme A synthase, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of HMG-CoA synthase enzymes from both eukaryotes and prokaryotes.

;

Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase ([ec:2.3.3.10]) catalyses the condensation of acetyl-CoA with acetoacetyl-CoA to produce HMG-CoA and CoA, the second reaction in the mevalonate-dependent isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway. HMG-CoA synthase contains an important catalytic cysteine residue that acts as a nucleophile in the first step of the reaction: the acetylation of the enzyme by acetyl-CoA (its first substrate) to produce an acetyl-enzyme thioester, releasing the reduced coenzyme A. The subsequent nucleophilic attack on acetoacetyl-CoA (its second substrate) leads to the formation of HMG-CoA [[cite:PUB00036056]].

HMG-CoA synthase occurs in eukaryotes, archaea and certain bacteria [[cite:PUB00036057]]. In vertebrates, there are two isozymes located in different subcellular compartments: a cytosolic form that is the starting point of the mevalonate pathway (leads to cholesterol and other sterolic and isoprenoid compounds), and a mitochondrial form responsible for ketone body biosynthesis. HMG-CoA is also found in other eukaryotes such as insects, plants and fungi [[cite:PUB00036058]]. In bacteria, isoprenoid precursors are generally synthesised via an alternative, non-mevalonate pathway, however a number of Gram-positive pathogens utilise a mevalonate pathway involving HMG-CoA synthase that is parallel to that found in eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00036059], [cite:PUB00036060]].

Name: Thiolase-like
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents a structural domain with a thiolase-like 3-layer α/β/α topology. This domain usually occurs in two similar copies that are related by a pseudo-dyad, and which arose through duplication. The proteins in this entry can be split into two groups: those related to thiolase, and those related to chalcone synthase. The thiolase-like enzymes include:

  • Thiolase, where the topology of each domain is similar to the first domain of phosphoglucomutase [[cite:PUB00020434]]
  • Beta-ketoacyl-ACP synthases types I ([ec:2.3.1.41]), II ([ec:2.3.1.179]) [[cite:PUB00036842], [cite:PUB00019762]] and III ([ec:2.3.1.180])
  • Actinorhodin polyketide beta-ketoacyl synthases 1 and 2 [[cite:PUB00031547]]
  • Fatty oxidation complex beta subunit (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase; [ec:2.3.1.16]) [[cite:PUB00032244]]

The chalcone synthase-like enzymes include:

  • Chalcone synthase ([ec:2.3.1.74]) [[cite:PUB00014381]]
  • Ketoacyl-ACP synthase III (FabH; [ec:2.3.1.180]) [[cite:PUB00025721]]
  • Polyketide synthases [[cite:PUB00031426]]
  • 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA synthase ([ec:2.3.3.10]) [[cite:PUB00016103]]
