This superfamily represents the domain 1 found in phosphate acetyltransferase.

Name: Phosphate acetyltransferase
ShortDescription: Phosphate acetyltransferase ([ec:2.3.1.8]) catalyses the conversion of acetyl-CoA and phosphate to CoA and acetyl phosphate in the last two steps in the conversion of actetae to acetyl-CoA.

Name: Phosphate acetyl/butaryl transferase
ShortDescription:
This entry contains both phosphate acetyltransferase [ec:2.3.1.8]: Acetyl-CoA + phosphate = CoA + acetyl phosphate

and phosphate butaryltransferase [ec:2.3.1.19]: Butanoyl-CoA + phosphate = CoA + butanoyl phosphate

These enzymes catalyse the transfer of an acetyl or butaryl group to orthophosphate.

Name: Phosphate Acetyltransferase/Butyryltransferase
ShortDescription: The Phosphate Acetyltransferase and Butyryltransferase family comprises enzymes involved in acetate metabolism, catalyzing the reversible interconversion of acetyl-CoA and acetyl phosphate, as well as the conversion of butyryl-CoA to butyrate via butyryl phosphate. These enzymes play a key role in the energy metabolism and regulation of acetylation potential in various bacteria. Members of the family are characterized by a conserved C-terminal substrate-binding site and an N-terminal region important for quaternary structure. Some family members are also involved in the metabolism of ethanolamine, propionate, and 1,2-propanediol, contributing to bacterial survival and pathogenicity.

Name: Hydrogenase expression/formation protein, HupF/HypC
ShortDescription: The large subunit of [NiFe]-hydrogenase, as well as other nickel metalloenzymes, is synthesised as a precursor devoid of the metalloenzyme active site. This precursor then undergoes a complex post-translational maturation process that requires a number of accessory proteins. The hydrogenase expression/formation and maturation proteins (HupF/HypC) form a family of small proteins that are hydrogenase precursor-specific chaperones required for this maturation process [[cite:PUB00003839]]. They are believed to keep the hydrogenase precursor in a conformation accessible for metal incorporation [[cite:PUB00011027], [cite:PUB00014218]].

Name: Bacterial extracellular foldase PrsA
ShortDescription: The PrsA family proteins are essential foldases that play a pivotal role in protein secretion processes. They assist in the post-translocational extracellular folding of various secreted proteins. Members of the PrsA family are involved in the production of active forms of enzymes and toxins, contributing to the stability and function of these extracellular proteins. Some members have peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) activity, although this is not always essential for their function in vivo. The PrsA proteins may exhibit different substrate specificities, indicating a degree of functional specialization within the family.

Name: Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase, PpiC-type, conserved site
ShortDescription:
Peptidylprolyl isomerase ([ec:5.2.1.8]) is an enzyme that accelerates protein folding by catalyzing the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides [[cite:PUB00000320]]. It has been reported in bacteria and eukayotes.

Synonyms for proteins with this domain are: Peptidylprolyl isomerase, Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase, PPIase, rotamase, cyclophilin, FKBP65.

Name: Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase, PpiC-type
ShortDescription:
Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase ([ec:5.2.1.8]) (PPIase or rotamase) is an enzyme that accelerates protein folding by catalysing the cis-trans isomerisation of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides [[cite:PUB00000320]]. Most characterised PPiases belong to two families, the cyclophilin-type and the the FKBP-type. A third family has been discovered [[cite:PUB00001678]]. So far, the only biochemically characterised member of this family is the Escherichia coli protein parvulin (gene ppiC), a small (92 residues) cytoplasmic enzyme that prefers amino acid residues with hydrophobic side chains like leucine and phenylalanine in the P1 position of the peptides substrates.

This entry represents a conserved region that contains a serine which could play a role in the catalytic mechanism of these enzymes. This domain is present in Periplasmic chaperone PpiD that were originally thought to be peptidyl-prolyl isomerases but it was shown later that they lack such activity [[cite:PUB00097266]].

Name: Acetolactate synthase/Transcription factor NikR, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This superfamily represent the C-terminal domain of the small subunit of acetolactate synthase and the C-terminal domain of the NikR, which is a transcription factor that regulates nickel uptake.

Name: Acetolactate synthase, small subunit
ShortDescription:
Acetolactate synthases are a group of biosynthetic enzymes apparently found in plants, fungi and bacteria that are capable ofde novosynthesis of the branched-chain amino acids [[cite:PUB00033863]]. They can all synthesize acetolactate from pyruvate in the biosynthesis of valine, while some are also capable of synthesizing acetohydroxybutyrate from pyruvate and ketobutyrate during the biosynthesis of isoleucine. These enzymes generally require thiamin diphosphate, FAD and a divalent metal ion for catalysis, though some enzymes specific for acetolactate synthesis do not require FAD. They are composed of two subunits, a large catalytic subunit, and a smaller regulatory subunit which binds the natural modulators (valine, and in some cases leucine or isoleucine).

These enzymes are the target for currently-used herbicides such as sulphonylureas and imidazolinones. Their restricted distribution also makes them potential targets for the development of novel antibacterial and antifungal compounds.

This entry represents the small regulatory subunit of acetolactate synthase. It contains an ACT domain, which is a predicted regulatory ligand-binding fold often found in proteins regulated by small-molecule effectors [[cite:PUB00007206]].

Name: Acetolactate synthase small subunit-like, ACT domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the ACT domain found at the N-terminal of acetohydroxyacid synthase isozyme III small subunit (ILVH) from Escherichia coli and at the C-terminal of D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase [[cite:PUB00005737], [cite:PUB00038467]], which are closely related [[cite:PUB00040493], [cite:PUB00154455], [cite:PUB00048655], [cite:PUB00154456]]. ILVH is the regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS), an enzyme that catalyses the first step in the biosynthesis of the three branched-chain amino acids [[cite:PUB00040493], [cite:PUB00154456]].

Name: Acetolactate synthase, small subunit, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of the small subunit of acetolactate synthase (the N-terminal domain being an ACT domain). Acetolactate synthase is a tetrameric enzyme, composed of two large and two small subunits, which catalyses the first step in branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis. This reaction is sensitive to certain herbicides [[cite:PUB00044146]].

Name: AHAS, ACT domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal ACT domain of the Escherichia coli IlvH-like regulatory subunit of acetolactate synthase (acetohydroxyacid synthase; AHAS). AHAS catalyses the first common step in the biosynthesis of the three branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine). The first step involves the condensation of either pyruvate or 2-ketobutyrate with the two-carbon hydroxyethyl fragment derived from another pyruvate molecule, covalently bound to the coenzyme thiamine diphosphate. Bacterial AHASs generally consist of regulatory and catalytic subunits. The effector (valine) binding sites are proposed to be located in two symmetrically related positions in the interface between a pair of N-terminal ACT domains with the C-terminal domain of IlvH contacting the catalytic dimer. Plants Arabidopsis and Oryza have tandem IlvH subunits; both the first and second ACT domain sequences are present in this entry [[cite:PUB00040493]].

Name: FlaG protein
ShortDescription: This entry includes protein FlaG (encoded from the flagellin locus) and an uncharacterised protein, YvyC, whose structure has been solved [[cite:PUB00069751]]. In Aeromonas caviae, mutation of FlaG does not affect motility but does significantly reduce the level of its adherence to HEp-2 cells [[cite:PUB00078328]].

Name: FlaG-like superfamily
ShortDescription: This entry includes protein FlaG (encoded from the flagellin locus) and an uncharacterised protein, YvyC, whose structure has been solved [[cite:PUB00069751]]. In Aeromonas caviae, mutation of FlaG does not affect motility but does significantly reduce the level of its adherence to HEp-2 cells [[cite:PUB00078328]].

Name: Metal-sensitive repressor, helix protomer superfamily
ShortDescription: The overall protomer fold consists of three α-helices of varying lengths, organised in a closed tetrameric assembly [[cite:PUB00097469]]. This superfamily includes metal-sensitive repressors involved in resistance to metal ions. Members of this superfamily bind copper, nickel or cobalt ions via conserved cysteine and histidine residues. In the absence of metal ions, these proteins bind to promoter regions and repress transcription. When bound to metal ions they are unable to bind DNA, leading to transcriptional derepression [[cite:PUB00041403], [cite:PUB00057455], [cite:PUB00057456], [cite:PUB00057457], [cite:PUB00035608]].

Name: Metal-sensitive transcriptional repressor
ShortDescription: This is a family of metal-sensitive repressors, involved in resistance to metal ions. Members of this family bind copper, nickel or cobalt ions via conserved cysteine and histidine residues. In the absence of metal ions, these proteins bind to promoter regions and repress transcription. When bound to metal ions they are unable to bind DNA, leading to transcriptional derepression [[cite:PUB00041403], [cite:PUB00057455], [cite:PUB00057456], [cite:PUB00057457], [cite:PUB00035608]].

Name: DegT/DnrJ/EryC1/StrS aminotransferase
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the 3-amino-5-hydroxybenzoic acid synthase family (AHBA_syn) that are probably all pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent aminotransferase enzymes with a variety of molecular functions. Members of the family have the same structural fold as members of the pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent aspartate aminotransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00023569]].

The AHBA_syn family members are involved in various biosynthetic pathways for secondary metabolites. The AHBA_synfamily includes StsA [swissprot:P72454], StsC [swissprot:P77952] and StsS [[cite:PUB00008019]]. The aminotransferase activity was demonstrated for purified StsC protein as the L-glutamine:scyllo-inosose aminotransferase [ec:2.6.1.50], which catalyses the first amino transfer in the biosynthesis of the streptidine subunit of streptomycin [[cite:PUB00008019]]. Some other well studied proteins in this family are AHBA_synthase, the protein product of the pleiotropic regulatory gene degT, Arnb aminotransferase and pilin glycosylation protein. The prototype of this family, the AHBA_synthase, is a dimeric PLP dependent enzyme.

AHBA_syn is the terminal enzyme of 3-amino-5-hydroxybenzoic acid (AHBA) formation, which is involved in the biosynthesis of ansamycin antibiotics, including rifamycin B. Some members of this family are involved in 4-amino-6-deoxy-monosaccharide D-perosamine synthesis. Perosamine is an important element in the glycosylation of several cell products, such as antibiotics and lipopolysaccharides of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. The pilin glycosylation protein encoded by gene pglA, is a galactosyltransferase involved in pilin glycosylation. Additionally, this family consists of ArnB (PmrH) aminotransferase, a 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose lipopolysaccharide-modifying enzyme. This family also includes several predicted pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzymes apparently involved in regulation of cell wall biogenesis. The catalytic lysine which is present in all characterised PLP dependent enzymes is replaced by histidine in some members of this family [[cite:PUB00028947], [cite:PUB00050697], [cite:PUB00039920], [cite:PUB00042185], [cite:PUB00008019], [cite:PUB00006322], [cite:PUB00016898], [cite:PUB00016775], [cite:PUB00006531], [cite:PUB00079514], [cite:PUB00035507], [cite:PUB00079515], [cite:PUB00070977]].

Name: AP-4-A phosphorylase
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in the catabolism of diadenosine polyphosphates. Specifically, they catalyse the breakdown of diadenosine 5',5'''-P1,P4-tetraphosphate (Ap4A) into adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). These enzymes prefer substrates that are dinucleoside polyphosphates with four or five phosphate residues. They are characterised by their inability to perform the reverse reaction, which is the synthesis of Ap4A from ADP and ATP.

Name: HIT-like domain
ShortDescription:
The histidine triad motif (HIT) consists of the conserved sequence HXHXHXX (where X is a hydrophobic amino acid) at the enzymatic catalytic centre, in which the second histidine is strictly conserved and participates in catalysis with the third histidine [[cite:PUB00097344], [cite:PUB00097347], [cite:PUB00008005]]. Proteins containing HIT domains form a superfamily of nucleotide hydrolases and transferases that act on the alpha-phosphate of ribonucleotides [[cite:PUB00008005], [cite:PUB00097344]]. They are highly conserved from archaea to humans and are involved in galactose metabolism, DNA repair, and tumor suppression [[cite:PUB00097349]]. HIT-containing proteins can be divided in five families based on catalytic specificities, sequence compositions, and structural similarities of its members:

  • Hint family of protein kinase-interacting proteins, the most ancient class in this superfamily. These include adenosine 5'-monophosphoramide hydrolases (e.g. HIT-nucleotide-binding protein, or HINT) [[cite:PUB00097345], [cite:PUB00008005]]. They also have a conserved zinc-binding motif C-X-X-C (where C is a cysteine residue and X is a hydrophobic residue), and a zinc ion is coordinated by these cysteine residues, together with the first histidine residue [[cite:PUB00097349]].
  • Fragile HIT protein, or FINT, whose name is due to its high rate of mutation at its locus on chromosome 3 in many cancers has been characterised as a tumor suppressor and plays a role in the hydrolysis of dinucleotide polyphosphates [[cite:PUB00097347], [cite:PUB00097349]]. HINT and FINT HIT domains have a topology similar to that found in the N-terminal of protein kinases [[cite:PUB00035586]].
  • GalT family. These include specific nucleoside monophosphate transferases (e.g. galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, diadenosine tetraphosphate phosphorylase, and adenylyl sulphate:phosphate adenylytransferase). These HIT domains are a duplication consisting of 2 HIT-like motifs. This family binds zinc and iron [[cite:PUB00097347], [cite:PUB00097343]].
  • Aprataxin, which hydrolyses both dinucleotide polyphosphates and phophoramidates, and is involved in DNA repair systems [[cite:PUB00097347], [cite:PUB00097349]].
  • mRNA decapping enzyme family. These include enzymes such as DcpS and Dcp2. The HIT-domain is usually C-terminal in these proteins [[cite:PUB00035587], [cite:PUB00097346]].

Name: FHIT family
ShortDescription: FHIT (fragile histidine) proteins are related to the HIT family members that carry a motif HxHxH/Qxx (x, is a hydrophobic amino acid) [[cite:PUB00005228]]. On the basis of sequence, substrate specificity, structure, evolution and mechanism, HIT proteins are classified into three branches: the Hint branch, which consists of adenosine 5' -monophosphoramide hydrolases, the FHIT branch, that consists of diadenosine polyphosphate hydrolases, and the GalT branch consisting of specific nucloside monophosphate transferases [[cite:PUB00008005], [cite:PUB00001122], [cite:PUB00008004]]. FHIT plays a very important role in the development of tumours. In fact, FHIT deletions are among the earliest and most frequent genetic alterations in the development of tumours [[cite:PUB00015781], [cite:PUB00089564]].

Name: UxaA family altronate/galactarate dehydratases
ShortDescription: The UxaA family encompasses enzymes that catalyze various dehydration reactions in bacterial metabolism. Members of the UxaA family are involved in the dehydration of D-altronate and galactarate, yielding their respective dehydrated products. Some UxaA family proteins function in concert with other subunits, such as the desulfonation of sulfolactate to produce pyruvate and sulfite. The family is characterized by a conserved domain structure, with some members having a domain that likely participates in substrate recognition and another domain implicated in dimerization and catalytic activity, potentially including metal binding. The activity of some UxaA enzymes can be inhibited by high concentrations of Fe(2+) or by chelating agents like EDTA.

Name: SAF domain
ShortDescription: This entry includes a range of different proteins, such as antifreeze proteins, flagellar FlgA proteins, and CpaB pilus proteins [[cite:PUB00017194]]. This domain adopts a β-clip fold [[cite:PUB00089354], [cite:PUB00095186]].

Name: UxaA/GarD, SAF domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the SAF domain found in altronate dehydratase UxaA and related proteins. UxaA converts D-altronate into 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate and is part of a bacterial pathway for the degradation of D-galacturonate. D-galactarate dehydratase eliminates water from D-galactarate to yield 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate, initializing the degradation of D-galactarate. The function of the SAF domain in these enzymes is not clear. It may participate in dimerization [[cite:PUB00009934], [cite:PUB00017194]].

This domain can also be found in galactarate dehydratase GarD, which catalyses the dehydration of galactarate to form 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-glucarate (5-KDG). The N-terminal SAF domain of GarD has been shown to form a β-clip fold [[cite:PUB00095186]].

Name: Truncated hemoglobin
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a group of haemoglobin-like proteins found in eubacteria, cyanobacteria, protozoa, algae and plants, but not in animals or yeast. These proteins have a truncated 2-over-2 rather than the canonical 3-over-3 α-helical sandwich fold [[cite:PUB00035871]]. They include:

  • HbN (or GlbN): a truncated haemoglobin-like protein that binds oxygen cooperatively with a very high affinity and a slow dissociation rate, which may exclude it from oxygen transport. It appears to be involved in bacterial nitric oxide detoxification and in nitrosative stress [[cite:PUB00035878]].
  • Cyanoglobin (or GlbN): a truncated haemoprotein found in cyanobacteria that has high oxygen affinity, and which appears to serve as part of a terminal oxidase, rather than as a respiratory pigment [[cite:PUB00035880]].
  • HbO (or GlbO): a truncated haemoglobin-like protein with a lower oxygen affinity than HbN. HbO associates with the bacterial cell membrane, where it significantly increases oxygen uptake over membranes lacking this protein. HbO appears to interact with a terminal oxidase, and could participate in an oxygen/electron-transfer process that facilitates oxygen transfer during aerobic metabolism [[cite:PUB00035879]].
  • Glb3: a nuclear-encoded truncated haemoglobin from plants that appears more closely related to HbO than HbN. Glb3 from Arabidopsis thaliana (Mouse-ear cress) exhibits an unusual concentration-independent binding of oxygen and carbon dioxide [[cite:PUB00035881]].
;

The truncated haemoglobin (trHb) family branches into three main groups, designated as type I, II and III and named as HbN, HbO and HbP, respectively. The trHbO gene (also known as glbO) has been predicted as the ancestral gene, with group I and group III genes appearing as a result of duplication and transfer events. There is an accumulating evidence suggests that trHbs may be implicated in functions other than oxygen delivery [[cite:PUB00153745]].

Name: Protein of unknown function DUF465
ShortDescription: Family members are found in small bacterial proteins, and also in the heavy chains of fungal proteins that contain the domain kinesin, in which this region is located C-terminal of the motor domain. Members of this family may form coiled coil structures [[cite:PUB00038888]].

Name: DUF465 superfamily
ShortDescription: Family members are found in small bacterial proteins, and also in the heavy chains of fungal proteins that contain the domain kinesin, in which this region is located C-terminal of the motor domain. Members of this family may form coiled coil structures [[cite:PUB00038888]].

Name: Glutathionylspermidine synthase, pre-ATP-grasp-like domain
ShortDescription: Glutathionylspermidine (GSP) synthetases of Trypanosomatidae and Escherichia coli couple hydrolysis of ATP (to ADP and Pi) with formation of an amide bond between spermidine and the glycine carboxylate of glutathione (gamma-Glu-Cys-Gly). In the pathogenic trypanosomatids, this reaction is the penultimate step in the biosynthesis of the antioxidant metabolite, trypanothione (N1,N8-bis-(glutathionyl)spermidine), and is a target for drug design [[cite:PUB00008407]]. This domain, which is structurally related to the pre-ATP grasp domain, probably carries the substrate-binding site [[cite:PUB00041749]].

Name: Aminotransferase class IV
ShortDescription:
Aminotransferases share certain mechanistic features with other pyridoxal-phosphate dependent enzymes, such as the covalent binding of the pyridoxal-phosphate group to a lysine residue. On the basis of sequence similarity, these various enzymes can be grouped [[cite:PUB00002195]] into subfamilies.

;

This entry represents a subfamily of aminotransferases, called class-IV, with currently consists of proteins of about 270 to 415 amino-acid residues that share a few regions of sequence similarity. Surprisingly, the best conserved region does not include the lysine residue to which the pyridoxal-phosphate group is known to be attached, in ilvE, but is located some 40 residues at the C terminus side of the pyridoxal-phosphate-lysine. The D-amino acid transferases (D-AAT), which are among the members of this entry, are required by bacteria to catalyse the synthesis of D-glutamic acid and D-alanine, which are essential constituents of bacterial cell wall and are the building block for other D-amino acids. Despite the difference in the structure of the substrates, D-AATs and L-ATTs have strong similarity [[cite:PUB00000425], [cite:PUB00002360]].

Bifunctional aminodeoxychorismate lyase / D-amino acid transaminase from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (also referred to as Rv0812) is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyses two enzymatic reactions in biochemically unrelated pathways: acts as an aminodeoxychorismate (ADC) lyase (ADCL) in folate biosynthesis, converting 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate (ADC) to 4-aminobenzoate (PABA), and as a D-amino acid transaminase (DAAT) in peptidoglycan (PG) biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00151494]].

This group also includes transaminase htyB from Aspergillus rugulosus, which is one of the enzymes required for the biosynthesis of the antifungal agent echinocandin B. HtyB catalyses the production of L-homotyrosine from the intermediate 2-oxo-4-(4-hydroxybenzyl)butanoic acid [[cite:PUB00088724]]. Also included in this group is branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase gloG from the yeast Glarea lozoyensis, which is required for biosynthesis of the mycotoxin pneumocandin, also a lipohexapeptide of the echinocandin family [[cite:PUB00089640]].

Name: Branched-chain-amino-acid aminotransferase-like, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the C-terminal large domain of BCATs.

;

Branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT) catalyses the transamination of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine to their respective alpha-keto acids, alpha-ketoisocaproate, alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate and alpha-ketoisovalerate. The enzyme requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor to catalyse the reaction. It has been found that mammals have two forms of the enzyme - mitochondrial and cytosolic forms, while bacteria contain only one form of the enzyme [[cite:PUB00081811]]. BCATs belong to the class 4 type aminotransferases and are widely distributed in many species [[cite:PUB00093722]]. Structurally, BCAT comprises two domains, the small domain consists of 7 β-strands and 3 α-helices, the large domain contains 6 β-strands and 3 α-helices [[cite:PUB00093722]].

ShortDescription: Branched-chain aminotransferase catalyses the transamination of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine to their respective alpha-keto acids, alpha-ketoisocaproate, alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate and alpha-ketoisovalerate. The enzyme requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor to catalyze the reaction. It has been found that mammals have two forms of the enzyme - mitochondrial and cytosolic forms while bacteria contain only one form of the enzyme [[cite:PUB00081811]]. The mitochondrial form plays a significant role in skeletal muscle glutamine and alanine synthesis and in interorgan nitrogen metabolism [[cite:PUB00081812]]. Members of this entry are widely distributed in all three forms of life.

Name: Branched-chain-amino-acid aminotransferase-like, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal small domain of BCATs [[cite:PUB00081811]].

Name: Branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase I
ShortDescription:

One of these, called class-IV, currently consists of proteins of about 270 to 415 amino-acid residues that share a few regions of sequence similarity. Surprisingly, the best conserved region does not include the lysine residue to which the pyridoxal-phosphate group is known to be attached, in ilvE, but is located some 40 residues at the C terminus side of the PlP-lysine.

Among the class IV aminotransferases are two phylogenetically separable groups of branched-chain amino acid aminotransferase (IlvE) ([ec:2.6.1.42]). The last common ancestor of the two lineages appears also to have given rise to a family of D-amino acid aminotransferases (DAAT). This model represents the IlvE family more strongly similar to the DAAT family.

Name: Aminotransferase-like, PLP-dependent enzymes
ShortDescription:
The D-amino acid transferases (D-AAT) are required by bacteria to catalyse the synthesis of D-glutamic acid and D-alanine, which are essential constituents of bacterial cell wall and are the building block for other D-amino acids [[cite:PUB00000425], [cite:PUB00002360]].

D-aminoacid aminotransferase is a homo hexamer with D3 symmetry, folded into two domains [[cite:PUB00002360]]. The first one has a beta3-alpha2-beta2 fold, while the second one has an α/β fold.

Name: Class-IV Pyridoxal-Phosphate-Dependent Aminotransferase
ShortDescription: The Class-IV Pyridoxal-Phosphate-Dependent Aminotransferase family comprises enzymes that catalyze the transfer of amino groups from amino acids to alpha-keto acids via a ping-pong mechanism. Members of this family are involved in the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids such as leucine, isoleucine, and valine, as well as D-amino acids including D-alanine, D-leucine, D-aspartate, D-glutamate, D-aminobutyrate, D-norvaline, and D-asparagine. These enzymes play crucial roles in processes such as the synthesis of bacterial cell wall components and the biosynthesis of p-aminobenzoate (PABA), a precursor of tetrahydrofolate. The family includes both specific branched-chain-amino-acid aminotransferases and D-alanine aminotransferases, as well as multifunctional enzymes with aminodeoxychorismate lyase activity, contributing to folate biosynthesis.

Name: Thioredoxin
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the thioredoxin protein family.

;

Thioredoxins [[cite:PUB00000038], [cite:PUB00002504], [cite:PUB00005258], [cite:PUB00005259]] are small disulphide-containing redox proteins that have been found in all the kingdoms of living organisms. Thioredoxin serves as a general protein disulphide oxidoreductase. It interacts with a broad range of proteins by a redox mechanism based on reversible oxidation of two cysteine thiol groups to a disulphide, accompanied by the transfer of two electrons and two protons. The net result is the covalent interconversion of a disulphide and a dithiol. In the NADPH-dependent protein disulphide reduction, thioredoxin reductase (TR) catalyses the reduction of oxidised thioredoxin (trx) by NADPH using FAD and its redox-active disulphide; reduced thioredoxin then directly reduces the disulphide in the substrate protein [[cite:PUB00000038]].

Thioredoxin is present in prokaryotes and eukaryotes and the sequence around the redox-active disulphide bond is well conserved. All thioredoxins contain a cis-proline located in a loop preceding β-strand 4, which makes contact with the active site cysteines, and is important for stability and function [[cite:PUB00005250]]. Thioredoxin belongs to a structural family that includes glutaredoxin, glutathione peroxidase, bacterial protein disulphide isomerase DsbA, and the N-terminal domain of glutathione transferase [[cite:PUB00005259]]. Thioredoxins have a β-α unit preceding the motif common to all these proteins.

A number of eukaryotic proteins contain domains evolutionary related to thioredoxin, most of them are protein disulphide isomerases (PDI). PDI ([ec:5.3.4.1]) [[cite:PUB00000561], [cite:PUB00001495], [cite:PUB00005423]] is an endoplasmic reticulum multi-functional enzyme that catalyses the formation and rearrangement of disulphide bonds during protein folding [[cite:PUB00002862]]. All PDI contains two or three (ERp72) copies of the thioredoxin domain, each of which contributes to disulphide isomerase activity, but which are functionally non-equivalent [[cite:PUB00002883]]. Moreover, PDI exhibits chaperone-like activity towards proteins that contain no disulphide bonds, i.e. behaving independently of its disulphide isomerase activity [[cite:PUB00001458]]. The various forms of PDI which are currently known are:

  • PDI major isozyme; a multifunctional protein that also function as the beta subunit of prolyl 4-hydroxylase ([ec:1.14.11.2]), as a component of oligosaccharyl transferase ([ec:2.4.1.119]), as thyroxine deiodinase ([ec:3.8.1.4]), as glutathione-insulin transhydrogenase ([ec:1.8.4.2]) and as a thyroid hormone-binding protein
  • ERp60 (ER-60; 58 Kd microsomal protein). ERp60 was originally thought to be a phosphoinositide-specific phospholipase C isozyme and later to be a protease.
  • ERp72.
  • ERp5.

Bacterial proteins that act as thiol:disulphide interchange proteins that allows disulphide bond formation in some periplasmic proteins also contain a thioredoxin domain. These proteins include:

  • Escherichia coli DsbA (or PrfA) and its orthologs in Vibrio cholerae (TtcpG) and Haemophilus influenzae (Por).
  • E. coli DsbC (or XpRA) and its orthologues in Erwinia chrysanthemi and H. influenzae.
  • E. coli DsbD (or DipZ) and its H. influenzae orthologue.
  • E. coli DsbE (or CcmG) and orthologues in H. influenzae.
  • Rhodobacter capsulatus (Rhodopseudomonas capsulata) (HelX), Rhiziobiacae (CycY and TlpA).

Name: Thioredoxin, conserved site
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a conserved site found in the thioredoxin domain. This site contains two cysteines that form the redox-active disulphide bond.

Name: Thioredoxin reductase
ShortDescription: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are known mediators of intracellular signalling cascades. Excessive production of ROS may, however, lead to oxidative stress, loss of cell function, and ultimately apoptosis or necrosis. A balance between oxidant and antioxidant intracellular systems is hence vital for cell function, regulation, and adaptation to diverse growth conditions. Thioredoxin reductase in conjunction with thioredoxin is a ubiquitous oxidoreductase system with antioxidant and redox regulatory roles. Thioredoxin reductase ([ec:1.8.1.9]) reduces oxidised thioredoxin in the presence of NADPH. Reduced thioredoxin serves as an electron donor for thioredoxin peroxidase which consequently reduces H2O2to H2O. In mammals, extracellular forms of Trx also have cytokine-like effects. Mammalian TrxR has a highly reactive active site selenocysteine residue resulting in a profound reductive capacity, reducing several substrates in addition to Trx [[cite:PUB00033166]].

Name: Cj0814 flagellar-dependent secreted protein
ShortDescription: Members of this family including Cj0814 [swissprot:Q0PA76], restricted to the genus Campylobacter, appear not to be flagellar proteins, but depend on flagellar expression in order to be secreted and be found in culture supernatant.

Name: MTA/SAH nucleosidase
ShortDescription: This entry represents the enzyme 5'-methylthioadenosine/S-adenosylhomocysteine nucleosidase (MTA/SAH nucleosidase) ([ec:3.2.2.9]) which acts on its two substrates at the same active site. This enzyme is involved in the recycling of the components of S-adenosylmethionine after it has donated one of its two non-ribose sulphur ligands to an acceptor. In the case of 5'-methylthioadenosine this represents the first step of the methionine salvage pathway in bacteria [[cite:PUB00013756], [cite:PUB00013829]]. This enzyme is essential for bacterial metabolism, while is absent in mammals, showing potential for antibiotic design [[cite:PUB00050679], [cite:PUB00099944]].

Name: Domain of unknown function DUF6844
ShortDescription: This domain is found predominantly found in proteobacteria and campylobacteria, including the hypothetical protein FTT_1539c from Francisella tularensis ([swissprot:Q5NES5]). It is located in the centre of the proteins included in this entry.

Name: Ferritin-like
ShortDescription: This entry represents ferritin and structurally related proteins. Ferritin is a major non-haem iron storage protein in animal, plants and microorganisms [[cite:PUB00016335]]. Iron is required by most organisms, but is potentially toxic due to its reactivity, which is counteracted by sequestering it into ferritin. Ferritin consists of a 4-helical bundle core, and contains a bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle. Other proteins with this structure include: haem-containing bacteriferritins; rubrerythrin, which appears to have a role in anaerobic detoxification pathway for reactive oxygen species [[cite:PUB00016336]]; Dps (DNA-binding proteins from starved cells) used in bacteria for iron storage-detoxification; and CRD1 (AcsF), which is required for the maintenance of photosystem I [[cite:PUB00015567]].

Name: Rubrerythrin, diiron-binding domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal diiron-binding domain of Rr, which has a has a ferritin-like fold [[cite:PUB00008767]].

;

Rubrerythrin (Rr) is a fusion protein containing an N-terminal diiron-binding domain and a C-terminal domain homologous to rubredoxin [[cite:PUB00002663]]. This protein has been related to the response to oxidative stress [[cite:PUB00100839], [cite:PUB00100840], [cite:PUB00098338]].

;

The 3-D structure of Desulphovibrio vulgaris rubrerythrin has been solved [[cite:PUB00008767]]. The structure reveals a tetramer of two-domain subunits. In each monomer, the N-terminal 146 residues form a four-α-helix bundle containing the diiron-oxo site (centre I), and the C-terminal 45 residues form a rubredoxin-like FeS4 domain.

Name: Desulfoferrodoxin, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Desulfoferrodoxin (class I) is a homodimeric protein, with each protomer comprised of two domains, the N-terminal desulforedoxin (DSRD) domain and C-terminal superoxide reductase-like (SORL) domain. Each domain has a distinct iron centre: the DSRD iron centre I, Fe(S-Cys)4; and the SORL iron centre II, Fe[His4Cys(Glu)] [[cite:PUB00015866]].

This entry represents the N-terminal desulforedoxin (DSRD) domain superfamilly. It has a similar fold to the rubredoxin metal binding domain.

Name: Desulfoferrodoxin, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
The desulforedoxin domain is a small non-haem iron domain present in the desulforedoxin (Dx) and desulfoferrodoxin (Superoxide reductase or Dfx) proteins of some archeael and bacterial methanogens and sulfate/sulfur reducers. It constitutes essentially the full length of desulforedoxin, and the N-terminal domain of Desulfoferrodoxin.

Desulforedoxin is a small, single-domain homodimeric protein. Each subunit (of 36 amino acid residues) contains an iron atom bound to four cysteinyl sulfur atoms, Fe(S-Cys)4, in a distorted tetrahedral coordination. Its metal centre is similar to that found in rubredoxin type proteins [[cite:PUB00016112]].

Name: Rubrerythrin, rubredoxin-like domain
ShortDescription:
Rubrerythrin (RUBY) is a fusion protein containing an N-terminal diiron-binding domain ([interpro:IPR003251]) and a C-terminal rubredoxin-like domain. RUBY may play a role in oxidative stress.

This entry represents the rubredoxin-like domain of RUBY, reverse rubrerythrin 1/2 from Clostridium acetobutylicum (RRBR1/2) and Nigerythrin from Desulfovibrio vulgaris [[cite:PUB00036376], [cite:PUB00018379], [cite:PUB00026588]]. RRBRs function as the terminal component of an NADH peroxidase when using NADH:rubredoxin oxidoreductase (NROR) as the electron transport intermediary from NADH to RRBRs and play an important role in the oxidative stress defence system of C. acetobutylicum [[cite:PUB00098338]].

Name: Ferritin-like diiron domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a group of proteins, containing ferritin-like domain, which is an about 145-residue domain made of a four-helix bundle surrounding a non-heme, non-sulphur, oxo-bridged diiron site. The diiron site is contained within a twisted, left-handed four-helix-bundle constituted of two anti-parallel helix pairs connected through a left-handed crossover connection. Known ligand residues at non-heme, non-sulphur diiron sites in proteins include His, Asp, Glu, and Tyr. Proteins containing a ferritin-like diiron domain possess the ability to catalyse oxidation of Fe2 to Fe3 by O2, i.e. ferroxidase activity. The ferritin-like diiron domain occurs in stand-alone form in ferritin and bacterioferritin or in association with the rubredoxin-like domain in rubrerythrin [[cite:PUB00008767]]. Proteins known to contain a ferritin-like diiron domain are listed below:

  • Ferritin (Ftn), an eukaryotic intracellular protein that stores iron in a soluble, nontoxic, readily available form.
  • Bacterioferritin (Bfr), a prokaryotic protein which may perform functions in iron detoxification and storage.
  • Rubrerythrin (Rr), a non-heme protein isolated from anaerobic sulphate- reducing bacteria.
  • Nigerythrin (Nr), a prokaryotic protein of unknown function.

Name: Rubrerythrin
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes rubrerythrin from Porphyromonas gingivalis, Clostridium perfringens and related sequences from bacteria and archaea. Rubrerythrin is involved in cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative stress. Members of this family are known to catalyse the reduction of hydrogen peroxide, thereby protecting the cell from the damaging effects of reactive oxygen species [[cite:PUB00100840]]. Some proteins within this family, such as rubrerythrin-1 from Clostridium acetobutylicum, function as part of an NADH peroxidase system, utilizing electron transport intermediaries to facilitate the reduction of hydrogen peroxide using NADH as an electron donor [[cite:PUB00098338]]. The activity of certain family members is enhanced by the presence of rubredoxin, which acts as an electron-transfer shuttle in the catalytic process.

Name: Ferritin-like superfamily
ShortDescription:
Ferritin is one of the major non-haem iron storage proteins in animals, plants, and microorganisms. It is a multisubunit protein with a hollow interior, which contains a mineral core of hydrated ferric oxide, thereby ensuring its solubility in an aqueous environment [[cite:PUB00013235]]. Each subunit consists of a closed, four-helical bundle with a left-handed twist and one crossover connection.

This entry represents the ferritin-like superfamily. Proteins with this structure include ferritin and other ferritin-like proteins such as bacterioferritin (cytochrome b1) that binds haem between two subunits, non-haem ferritin, dodecameric ferritin homologue (DPS) that binds to and protects DNA, and the N-terminal domain of rubrerythrin that is found in many air-sensitive bacteria and archaea [[cite:PUB00013236]]. In addition, ribonucleotide reductase-like proteins show a similar structure to the ferritin-like fold; these di-iron carboxylate proteins constitute a diverse class of non-haem iron enzymes performing a multitude of redox reactions [[cite:PUB00013315]]. The superfamily also includes the alpha and beta subunits of methane monooxygenase hydrolase, delta 9-stearoyl-acyl carrier protein desaturase and manganese catalase.

Name: Rubredoxin-like domain
ShortDescription:
Rubredoxin is a low molecular weight iron-containing bacterial protein involved in electron transfer [[cite:PUB00000489], [cite:PUB00003266]], sometimes replacing ferredoxin as an electron carrier [[cite:PUB00008022]]. Rubredoxins possess a 45- to 55-residue domain containing one iron atom tetrahedrally coordinated to four cysteinyl residues. Structural analysis of the domains have shown them to be folded into a short three-stranded antiparallel β-sheet and a number of loops [[cite:PUB00008024], [cite:PUB00008023], [cite:PUB00018378], [cite:PUB00008767]].

;

This entry represents rubredoxin-like domains, which are found in rubredoxins and related proteins, including rubrerythrins, flavorubredoxins and nigerythrins.

Name: Midasin AAA lid domain 5
ShortDescription: This entry represents the α helical AAA+ lid domain that is found to the C terminus of AAA domains [[cite:PUB00016211]]. This lid domain is found in midasin, which is a nuclear chaperone required for maturation and nuclear export of pre-60S ribosome subunits [[cite:PUB00091479]].

Name: Midasin, AAA lid domain 7
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the α helical AAA+ lid domain that is found to the C terminus of AAA domains. This lid domain is found in midasin proteins.

Midasin (MDN1, REA1) is a is a member of the AAA(+) family of ATPases. It is a nuclear chaperone required for maturation and nuclear export of pre-60S ribosome subunits [[cite:PUB00056113], [cite:PUB00056196], [cite:PUB00053246], [cite:PUB00073617]].

Name: ATPase, dynein-related, AAA domain
ShortDescription: The ATPases Associated to a variety of cellular Activities (AAA) are a family distinguished by a highly conserved module of 230 amino acids [[cite:PUB00000729]]. The highly conserved nature of this module across taxa suggests that it has a key cellular role. Members of the family are involved in diverse cellular functions including gene expression, peroxisome assembly and vesicle mediated transport. Although the role of this ATPase AAA domain is not, as yet, clear, the AAA+ superfamily of proteins to which the AAA ATPases belong has a chaperone-like function in the assembly, operation or disassembly of proteins [[cite:PUB00005841]]. This ATPase domain includes some proteins not detected by the [interpro:IPR003959] model.

Name: Midasin
ShortDescription: Midasin (MDN1, REA1) is a is a member of the AAA(+) family of ATPases. It is a nuclear chaperone required for maturation and nuclear export of pre-60S ribosome subunits [[cite:PUB00056113], [cite:PUB00056196], [cite:PUB00053246], [cite:PUB00073617]].

Name: Midasin, lid domain 4
ShortDescription: Mdn1 is an essential AAA (ATPase associated with various activities) protein that removes assembly factors from distinct precursors of the ribosomal 60S subunit [[cite:PUB00151693]]. This entry represents an AAA domain lid domain.

Name: WD repeat WDR12/Ytm1
ShortDescription: This entry represents the WD repeat WDR12/Ytm1 family. Members of this familiy are ribosome biogenesis proteins.

Name: Tricarboxylate/iron carrier
ShortDescription: The MTC family consists of a limited number of homologues, all from eukaryotes. One member of the family has been functionally characterised as a tricarboxylate carrier from rat liver mitochondria. The rat liver mitochondrial tricarboxylate carrier has been reported to transport citrate, cis-aconitate, threo-D-isocitrate, D- and L-tartrate, malate, succinate and phosphoenolpyruvate. It presumably functions by a proton symport mechanism. The rest of the characterised proteins appear to be sideroflexins involved in iron transport.

Name: 16S/18S rRNA aminocarboxypropyltransferase Tsr3, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This domain can be found in the eukaryotic ribosome biogenesis protein Tsr3, which is involved in ribosomal RNA biogenesis [[cite:PUB00076727]]. This domain is also found in the C terminus of Tsr3 homologues from archaea. It is usually associated with a putative metal-binding region in RNase L inhibitor, RLI ([interpro:IPR007209]).

Tsr3 from fungi and animals are responsible for 18S rRNA hypermodification. The Crystal structure of archaeal Tsr3 homologues revealed the same fold as in SPOUT-class RNA-methyltransferases but a distinct SAM binding mode. This unique SAM binding mode explains why Tsr3 transfers the acp and not the methyl group of SAM to its substrate. Structurally, Tsr3 therefore represents a novel class of acp transferase enzymes [[cite:PUB00094251]].

Name: RNase L inhibitor RLI-like, possible metal-binding domain
ShortDescription: This is part of a possible metal-binding domain in endoribonuclease RNase L inhibitor. It is found at the N-terminal end of RNase L inhibitor proteins, adjacent to the 4Fe-4S binding domain, [interpro:IPR017896]. Also often found adjacent to [interpro:IPR007177] in uncharacterised proteins. The RNase L system plays a major role in the anti-viral and anti-proliferative activities of interferons [[cite:PUB00009821]]. It is a component of the multifactor complex (MFC) involved in translation initiation and it is required for the processing and nuclear export of the 60S and 40S ribosomal subunits, playing a role in ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00096731], [cite:PUB00045430]. Inhibitory activity requires concentration-dependent association of RLI with RNase L [[cite:PUB00009822]].

Name: 16S/18S rRNA aminocarboxypropyltransferase Tsr3
ShortDescription: This entry represents18S rRNA aminocarboxypropyltransferases Tsr3 and its homologues. Tsr3 from fungi and animals are responsible for 18S rRNA hypermodification. It introduces the acp group to the hypermodified m1acp3psi nucleotide at position 1191 (yeast)/ 1248 (humans) of 18S rRNA. The crystal structure of archaeal Tsr3 homologues revealed the same fold as in SPOUT-class RNA-methyltransferases but a distinct SAM binding mode. This unique SAM binding mode explains why Tsr3 transfers the acp and not the methyl group of SAM to its substrate. Structurally, Tsr3 therefore represents a novel class of acp transferase enzymes [[cite:PUB00094251]].

Name: BRCT domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
The breast cancer susceptibility gene contains at its C terminus two copies of a conserved domain that was named BRCT for BRCA1 C terminus. This domain of about 95 amino acids is found in a large variety of proteins involved in DNA repair, recombination and cell cycle control [[cite:PUB00003902], [cite:PUB00001533], [cite:PUB00001703]]. The BRCT domain is not limited to the C-terminal of protein sequences and can be found in multiple copies or in a single copy as in RAP1 and TdT. Some data [[cite:PUB00001320]] indicate that the BRCT domain functions as a protein-protein interaction module.

The structure of the first of the two C-terminal BRCT domains of the human DNA repair protein XRCC1 has been determined by X-ray crystallography, it comprises a four-stranded parallel β-sheet surrounded by three α-helices, which form an autonomously folded domain [[cite:PUB00001320]].

Name: Chitin biosynthesis protein Chs5, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This domain is found at the N-terminal of the fungal chitin biosynthesis protein Chs5 [[cite:PUB00080389]]. It functions as a dimerisation domain [[cite:PUB00075986]].

;

Chs5/6 is a multi-protein complex conserved in fungi that interacts with chitin synthase III (Chs3p) and is involved in its transport to the cell surface from the trans-Golgi network, functioning as an exomer cargo adapter. Chs5p appears to form a complex with Chs6p and its paralogues Bch1p, Bud7p, and Bch2p. In this complex, Chs5p may act as a central scaffold [[cite:PUB00080390]]. The N-terminal domain characterised by this model forms a homodimer and has been shown to interact with Chs6p and Bch1p. It may function as a flexible hinge domain that allows the exomer to interact with both proteins and the Golgi membrane as the latter undergoes changes in curvature during the formation of transport vesicles [[cite:PUB00075986]]. The dimerisation domain sits N-terminally to a conserved FBE (FN3-BRCT) unit, which binds Arf1 and is involved in the recruitment of the exomer to the membrane [[cite:PUB00075985]].

Name: BRCT domain
ShortDescription:
The breast cancer susceptibility gene contains at its C terminus two copies of a conserved domain that was named BRCT for BRCA1 C terminus. This domain of about 95 amino acids is found in a large variety of proteins involved in DNA repair, recombination and cell cycle control [[cite:PUB00003902], [cite:PUB00001533], [cite:PUB00001703]]. The BRCT domain is not limited to the C-terminal of protein sequences and can be found in multiple copies or in a single copy as in RAP1 and TdT. BRCT domains are often found as tandem-repeat pairs [[cite:PUB00094292]]. Some data [[cite:PUB00001320]] indicate that the BRCT domain functions as a protein-protein interaction module.

The structure of the first of the two C-terminal BRCT domains of the human DNA repair protein XRCC1 has been determined by X-ray crystallography [[cite:PUB00001320]].

Structures of the BRCA1 BRCT domains revealed a basis for a widely utilised head-to-tail BRCT-BRCT oligomerisation mode [[cite:PUB00026458]]. This conserved tandem BRCT architecture facilitates formation of the canonical BRCT phospho-peptide interaction cleft at a groove between the BRCT domains. BRCT domains disrupt peptide binding by directly occluding this peptide binding groove, or by disrupting key conserved BRCT core folding determinants [[cite:PUB00031299]].

Name: Chitin Synthase Export/Cell Fusion Regulator
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in various cellular processes related to the synthesis of chitin and cell fusion. Members of this family are known to form complexes that facilitate the export of specific cargo proteins, such as chitin synthase, to their proper cellular locations. Additionally, they play a role in the targeting of proteins to sites of polarized growth. Some family members act as scaffolds within the Golgi apparatus, retaining proteins required for cell fusion. The degradation of these proteins can trigger the release of cell fusion proteins, indicating a regulatory function in mating processes. Overall, the family is characterized by its involvement in the transport and regulation of proteins essential for chitin biosynthesis and cell fusion events.

Name: Fibronectin type III domain, fungi
ShortDescription: This fibronectin type III domain is found in fungal chitin biosynthesis protein CHS5 where, together with the neighbouring BRCT domain ([interpro:IPR001357]), it binds to the Arf1 GTPase [[cite:PUB00075985]].

Name: CEBPZ/Mak21-like
ShortDescription: This represents CAATT-binding proteins and their homologues, including Mak21 from budding yeasts, protein SLOW WALKER2 (SWA2) from Arabidopsis and CEBPZ from human and its orthologue from Drosophila Nucleolar complex protein 1 (Noc1). Mak21, also known as Noc1, is required for 60 S ribosomal subunit biogenesis [[cite:PUB00019257]]. Together with Rrp5 and Noc2, Mak21 forms a protein module which is part of early large ribosomal subunit precursors [[cite:PUB00090618]]. SWA2 may play a role in ribosome biogenesis and is essential for coordinated cell cycle progression during female gametophyte development in Arabidopsis [[cite:PUB00090619]]. CEBPZ, the human homologue, regulates Hsp70 expression [[cite:PUB00019257]]. Noc1 from Drosophila is involved in rRNA processing and ribosome maturation[[cite:PUB00153394]].

Name: CCAAT-binding factor
ShortDescription: This domain is present in the CAATT-binding protein which is essential for growth and necessary for 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis. Other proteins containing this domain stimulate transcription from the HSP70 promoter.

Name: 26S Proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 12/COP9 signalosome complex subunit 4
ShortDescription:
The 26S proteasome consists of a 20S proteolytic core particle (CP) and a 19S regulatory particle (RP). The RP can be further divided into two subcomplexes, the base that directly associates with the CP and a peripheral lid. The RP lid is structurally similar to the COP9 signalosome (CSN). The core CSN subunits (CSN4/5/7/6) show a remarkable one-to-one sequence correspondence with those of the RP lid (RPN5/11/9/8), suggesting a common ancestry and architecture [[cite:PUB00033528]].

This family includes the 26S Proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 12 (PSMD12 or RPN5), a component of the 26S proteasome lid [[cite:PUB00085267]], and the COP9 signalosome subunit 4 [[cite:PUB00088094]].

Name: PSMD12/CSN4-like, N-terminal
ShortDescription: The 26S proteasome consists of a 20S proteolytic core particle (CP) and a 19S regulatory particle (RP). The RP can be further divided into two subcomplexes, a base and a peripheral lid. The RP lid is structurally similar to the COP9 signalosome (CSN). The core CSN subunits (CSN4/5/7/6) show a remarkable one-to-one sequence correspondence with those of the RP lid (RPN5/11/9/8), suggesting a common ancestry and architecture [[cite:PUB00033528]]. This entry represents the N-terminal region of PSMD12/RPN5 and CSN4 subunits, which consists of helical repeats [[cite:PUB00033528], [cite:PUB00110070], [cite:PUB00154186], [cite:PUB00091374], [cite:PUB00152659]].

Name: 26S proteasome regulatory subunit RPN5, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of the 26S proteasome regulatory subunit RPN5. This helical domain can be found adjacent to the PCI domain. The 26S proteasome is the major ATP-dependent protease in eukaryotes that consists of three subcomplexes: the lid, the base, and the core. The helices found at the C terminus of each lid subunit form a helical bundle that directs the ordered self-assembly of the lid subcomplex. This domain which comprises the tail of RPN5 along with the tail of RPN9, are important for RPN12 binding to the lid [[cite:PUB00091262]].

Name: WD repeat RBAP46/RBAP48/MSI1
ShortDescription: The WD repeat RBAP46/RBAP48/MSI1 family is involved in chromatin metabolism and regulation. Members of this family function as core histone-binding subunits targeting chromatin assembly factors, chromatin remodeling factors, and histone deacetylases to histone substrates, regulated by nucleosomal DNA. They are components of several complexes, including the type B histone acetyltransferase (HAT-B) complex for chromatin assembly post-DNA replication, the core histone deacetylase (HDAC) complex for transcriptional repression, the NuRD complex for transcriptional repression through histone deacetylation and nucleosome remodeling, and the PRC2/EED-EZH2 complex for homeotic gene repression during development. Additionally, they play roles in telomeric silencing, meiotic regulation, and various developmental processes by maintaining transcriptionally repressive states of genes.

Name: WD repeat Prp46/PLRG1-like
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of WD40 repeat containing proteins, including Prp46 from budding yeasts, Prp5 from fission yeasts, PLRG1 from animals and PRL1/2 from plants. Prp46 and Prp5 are involved in pre-mRNA splicing and may be required for both cell cycle progression at G2/M [[cite:PUB00098347], [cite:PUB00098346]]. PLRG1 is a component of the PRP19-CDC5L complex that forms an integral part of the spliceosome and is required for activating pre-mRNA splicing [[cite:PUB00098349], [cite:PUB00098348]]. In Arabidopsis PRL1/2 are pleiotropic regulator of glucose, stress and hormone responses [[cite:PUB00045255]]. PRL1 is part of the MAC, a multiprotein complex with a role in plant defense signaling [[cite:PUB00098350]].

Name: Nucleolar protein 10-like, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found at the N-terminal of human Nucleolar protein 10 (NOL10) and similar eukaryotic sequences including the orthologue from yeast Ribosome biogenesis protein (ENP2). This domain is normally found N-terminal to [interpro:IPR056550]. This entry includes a entire β-propeller structure and two α-helices.

;

NOL10 (also known as Polyglutamine binding protein 5 (PQBP5)) binds to polyglutamine tract sequences and is expressed in the nucleolus. It makes up the skeletal structure of the nucleolus, constituting the granule meshwork in the granular component area, and functions as an anchor for reassembly of other nucleolar proteins [[cite:PUB00158898]].

ENP2 was identified in a set of proteins involved in rRNA-processing and ribosome biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00075792]].

Name: Activator of Hsp90 ATPase homologue 1/2-like, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found in eukaryotic, prokaryotic and archaeal proteins that bear similarity to a C-terminal region of human activator of 90kDa heat shock protein ATPase homologue 1 (AHSA1/p38, [swissprot:O95433]) and Aha1 from yeast [[cite:PUB00102522], [cite:PUB00102523]]. This is a START-like domain (also referred to as SRPBCC domain which stands for START/RHO_alpha_C/PITP/Bet_v1/CoxG/CalC) which interacts with, and stabilizes the hydrophobic binding groove exposed after the interaction between the N-terminal domain of Aha1 ([interpro:IPR015310]) and the middle domain of Hsp90 [[cite:PUB00102523], [cite:PUB00102524]]. SRPBCC domains have a deep hydrophobic ligand-binding pocket. This domain is found repeated in two members of this entry ([SwissProt:Q8XY04] and [swissprot:Q6MH87]).

AHSA1/Aha1 are known to interact with the middle domain of Hsp90, and stimulate its ATPase activity [[cite:PUB00020903], [cite:PUB00102524]], one Aha1 molecule per Hsp90 dimer is sufficient for a full stimulation of Hsp90. It is probably a general up regulator of Hsp90 function, particularly contributing to its efficiency in conditions of increased stress [[cite:PUB00020879]]. AHSA1 is also known to interact with the cytoplasmic domain of the VSV G protein, and may thus be involved in protein transport [[cite:PUB00020832]]. It has also been reported as being under expressed in Down's syndrome.

Name: Activator of Hsp90 ATPase AHSA1-like, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry includes a group of heat shock protein interacting proteins, including AHSA1/2 from animals and Aha1/Hch1 from budding yeasts, and it represents a domain found at the N-terminal of Aha1 and AHSA1/2, while in Hch1 is the only domain. Aha1 adopts a secondary structure consisting of an N-terminal α-helix leading into a four-stranded meandering antiparallel β-sheet, followed by a C-terminal α-helix. The two α-helices are packed together, with the β-sheet curving around them. The N-terminal domain of Aha1 interacts with the central segment of Hsp90 which induces the conformational rearrangements of Hsp90 that favor the N-terminal domain-dimerized state of the chaperone and ends leads to the stimulation of its ATPase activity [[cite:PUB00035354]].

Activator of 90kDa heat shock protein ATPase Aha1/AHSA1 (AHSA1/p38, [swissprot:O95433]) is known to interact with the middle domain of Hsp90, and stimulate its ATPase activity [[cite:PUB00020903], [cite:PUB00102524]], where one Aha1/AHSA1 molecule per Hsp90 dimer is sufficient for this stimulation. It is probably a general up regulator of Hsp90 function, particularly contributing to its efficiency in conditions of increased stress [[cite:PUB00020879]]. It is also known to interact with the cytoplasmic domain of the VSV G protein, and may thus be involved in protein transport [[cite:PUB00020832]]. It has also been reported as being under expressed in Down's syndrome.

In budding yeasts, both Hch1 and Aha1 bind to the middle domain of Hsp90 and stimulate ATPase activity [[cite:PUB00020903], [cite:PUB00090459]]. However, Aha1 but not Hch1 stimulated the intrinsic ATPase activity of Hsp90 5-fold [[cite:PUB00020903]]. Hch1 and Aha1 may regulate Hsp90 function in distinct ways [[cite:PUB00020903]].

Name: Activator of Hsp90 ATPase, Aha1
ShortDescription: Aha1 is a co-chaperone that binds to the chaperone Hsp90 stimulating its ATPase activity. Aha1 adopts a secondary structure consisting of an N-terminal α-helix leading into a four-stranded meandering antiparallel β-sheet, followed by a C-terminal α-helix. The two α helices are packed together, with the β-sheet curving around them. The N-terminal domain of Aha1 interacts with Hsp90 and stimulates its ATPase activity [[cite:PUB00035354]].

Name: START-like domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents an α/β sandwich structural domain found in a wide variety of protein families, including STAR-related lipid transfer proteins and homeobox-leucine zipper proteins.

;

START (StAR-related lipid-transfer) is a lipid-binding domain in StAR, HD-ZIP and signalling proteins [[cite:PUB00005851]]. StAR (Steroidogenic Acute Regulatory protein) is a mitochondrial protein that is synthesised in response to luteinising hormone stimulation [[cite:PUB00002877]]. Expression of the protein in the absence of hormone stimulation is sufficient to induce steroid production, suggesting that this protein is required in the acute regulation of steroidogenesis. Representatives of the START domain family have been shown to bind different ligands such as sterols (StAR protein) and phosphatidylcholine (PC-TP). Ligand binding by the START domain can also regulate the activities of other domains that co-occur with the START domain in multidomain proteins such as Rho-gap, the homeodomain, and the thioesterase domain [[cite:PUB00005851], [cite:PUB00007207]].

Name: Nucleolar protein Nop56/Nop58
ShortDescription:
This entry includes a group of pre-RNA processing ribonucleoproteins (RNPs), including Nop56/Nop58 from animals and their homologue, Nop5, from archaea. Proteins in this family contains the Nop domain, which is a RNP binding module, exhibiting RNA and protein binding surfaces. It is oval-shaped and exclusively α-helical [[cite:PUB00027813], [cite:PUB00062919]].

;

Nucleolar protein 56 and 58 (NOP56/58) are required for 60S ribosomal subunit synthesis [[cite:PUB00003706]]. They are core components of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) particles [[cite:PUB00097816], [cite:PUB00090687], [cite:PUB00097817], [cite:PUB00097817]]. In humans, NOP56 is associated with a type of slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by late-onset ataxia followed by variable involvement of the motor neuron system [[cite:PUB00103405], [cite:PUB00103406]].

Name: Nop domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the Nop domain superfamily.

;

The Nop domain is present in various pre-RNA processing ribonucleoproteins (RNP):

  • Eukaryotic Prp31, part of a tri-snRNP complex. It is involved in pre-mRNA splicing.
  • Eukaryotic Nucleolar proteins 56 and 58 (Nop56 and Nop58), components of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) particles.
  • Archaeal Nop5, an homologue of Nop56/Nop58.

The Nop domain is a RNP binding module, exhibiting RNA and protein binding surfaces. It is oval-shaped and exclusively α-helical [[cite:PUB00027813], [cite:PUB00062919]].

;

U4/U6 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein Prp31 (PRPF31) is involved in pre-mRNA splicing as component of the spliceosome [[cite:PUB00044450], [cite:PUB00090272]]. This protein is required for the assembly of the U4/U5/U6 tri-snRNP complex, one of the building blocks of the spliceosome [[cite:PUB00044450]]. It is associated with a progressive pigmentary retinopathy characterised by night vision blindness and loss of midperipheral visual field [[cite:PUB00044451], [cite:PUB00062921]].

;

Nucleolar protein 56 and 58 (NOP56/58) are required for 60S ribosomal subunit synthesis [[cite:PUB00003706]]. They are core components of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) particles [[cite:PUB00097816], [cite:PUB00090687], [cite:PUB00097817], [cite:PUB00097817]]. In humans, NOP56 is associated with a type of slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by late-onset ataxia followed by variable involvement of the motor neuron system [[cite:PUB00103405], [cite:PUB00103406]].

Name: Nucleolar protein 58/56, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This N-terminal domain is found in Nucleolar protein 58/56 from fungi and animals and the homologues form plants. These are RNA-binding proteins of the NOP5 family [[cite:PUB00016366]]. Nop56 and Nop58 are components of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) particles [[cite:PUB00097816], [cite:PUB00097817]]. This domain interacts with Nop1 and forms the box B/C side, in the case of Nop56, or box C'/D side in the case of Nop58, of U3 snoRNP [[cite:PUB00101204]].

Name: Nop, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
The Nop domain is present in various pre-RNA processing ribonucleoproteins (RNP):

  • Eukaryotic Prp31, part of a tri-snRNP complex. It is involved in pre-mRNA splicing.
  • Eukaryotic Nucleolar proteins 56 and 58 (Nop56 and Nop58), components of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) particles.
  • Archaeal Nop5, an homologue of Nop56/Nop58.

Name: NOSIC
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain centrally located in a group of pre-RNA processing ribonucleoproteins (RNPs), including the eukaryotic proteins Prp31, Nop56 and Nop58 and the archaeal homologue Nop5. This domain was named after the central domain in Nop56/SIK1-like proteins [[cite:PUB00016366], [cite:PUB00103404]]. It is found associated with the Nop domain ([interpro:IPR002687]).

Name: Serine/threonine-protein kinase Atg1-like
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a group of Serine/threonine-protein kinases, including Atg1 from yeasts, Unc-51 from C. elegans, Ulk1-3 from humans and ATG1a/b/c/t from Arabidopsis.

Atg1 is required for vesicle formation in autophagy and the cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting (Cvt) pathway [[cite:PUB00066530]].

Ulk1-3 are involved in autophagy in response to starvation [[cite:PUB00098424], [cite:PUB00098425]]. Ulk1 and Ulk2 regulate filopodia extension and branching of sensory axons. They are important for axon growth, playing an essential role in neurite extension of cerebellar granule cells [[cite:PUB00042782], [cite:PUB00034854]].

Unc-51 is important for axonal elongation and axonal guidance [[cite:PUB00042769]]. It is required for either the maintenance of axons (membrane turnover) or for an unknown neuronal function. C elegans worms lacking Unc-51 exhibit various abnormalities in axonal elongation and axonal structures. Unc-51 could also help control cell size along with Bec-1, as mutations in their corresponding genes results in a reduction in small body size without affecting cell number [[cite:PUB00042770]]. Unc-51 is also a component of the Unc-51/Atg-13 complex that is probably recruited by lgg-1 to preautophagosomes and is required for autophagosome formation [[cite:PUB00098426]].

In plants, the ATG1/13 complex is both a regulator and a target of autophagy [[cite:PUB00098423]].

This family also includes the serine/threonine protein kinase Negative regulator of sexual conjugation and meiosis from Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Ran1 or Pat1), a negative regulator of both sexual conjugation and meiosis [[cite:PUB00162479]]

Name: WD repeat-containing DNA damage-binding protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes members that are involved in DNA-binding and recognition of specific DNA modifications. They are known to bind to both single- and double-stranded DNA, with a preference for UV-damaged DNA, suggesting a role in DNA repair and maintenance. Some family members have been identified as specific readers of the modified DNA base 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), which is important in epigenetic regulation. The presence of WD repeats indicates a potential role in protein-protein interactions, which may be crucial for their function in DNA-metabolic processes.

Name: Sec39 domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a Sec39 domain, which can be found in yeast Sec39, human NBAS (neuroblastoma-amplified sequence) [[cite:PUB00072937]] and Arabidopsis MIP2 (MAG2-INTERACTING PROTEIN 2) [[cite:PUB00072936]]. They may be involved in Golgi-to-ER transport.

Sec39 was originally identified as a protein involved in ER-Golgi transport in a large scale promoter shut down analysis of essential yeast genes [[cite:PUB00045128]]. A subsequent study found that Sec39p (Dsl3p) is required for Golgi-ER retrograde transport and is part of a very stable protein complex that also includes Dsl1p (in mammals ZW10), Tip20p (Rint-1) and the ER localized Q-SNARE proteins Ufe1p (syntaxin-18), Sec20p and Use1p [[cite:PUB00045128]]. This was confirmed in a genome-wide analysis of protein complexes [[cite:PUB00045129]].

Name: SWI/SNF Subunit INI1, DNA binding domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal winged helix DNA binding domain of the INI1/hSNF5/SMARCB1 subunit [[cite:PUB00151808]] and similar sequences from animals.

SWI/SNF complexes use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to remodel chromatin. In mammals they play a central role in regulating gene expression during differentiation and proliferation [[cite:PUB00151808]].

Name: TNF receptor-associated factor, BIRC3 binding domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in TNF receptor-associated factor 1 and 2 (TRAF1 and TRAF2), where it binds to Baculoviral IAP repeat-containing protein 3 (BIRC3) (cIAP2) [[cite:PUB00058706]].

Name: TRAF1-6, MATH domain
ShortDescription: Intracellular TRAFs and extracellular meprins share a conserved region of about 180 residues, the meprin and TRAF homology (MATH) domain which adopts a β-sandwich structure. This is the MATH domain of TNF receptor-associated factors 1-6 (TRAF1-6). In TRAFS, this domain is essential for self-association and receptor interaction [[cite:PUB00011815], [cite:PUB00058618], [cite:PUB00062992]].

Name: Zinc finger, C3HC4 RING-type
ShortDescription:
The C3HC4 type zinc-finger (RING finger) is a cysteine-rich domain of 40 to 60 residues that coordinates two zinc ions, and has the consensus sequence: C-X2-C-X(9-39)-C-X(1-3)-H-X(2-3)-C-X2-C-X(4-48)-C-X2-C where X is any amino acid [[cite:PUB00001094]]. Many proteins containing a RING finger play a key role in the ubiquitination pathway [[cite:PUB00017952]].

;

Zinc finger (Znf) domains are relatively small protein motifs which contain multiple finger-like protrusions that make tandem contacts with their target molecule. Some of these domains bind zinc, but many do not; instead, they bind other metals, such as iron, or no metal at all. For example, some family members form salt bridges to stabilise the finger-like folds. They were first identified as a DNA-binding motif in transcription factor TFIIIA from Xenopus laevis (African clawed frog); however, they are now recognised to bind DNA, RNA, protein and/or lipid substrates [[cite:PUB00035807], [cite:PUB00035805], [cite:PUB00035806], [cite:PUB00035804], [cite:PUB00014077]]. Their binding properties depend on the amino acid sequence of the finger domains and of the linker between fingers, as well as on the higher-order structures and the number of fingers. Znf domains are often found in clusters, where fingers can have different binding specificities. There are many superfamilies of Znf motifs, varying in both sequence and structure. They display considerable versatility in binding modes, even between members of the same class (e.g., some bind DNA, others protein), suggesting that Znf motifs are stable scaffolds that have evolved specialised functions. For example, Znf-containing proteins function in gene transcription, translation, mRNA trafficking, cytoskeleton organisation, epithelial development, cell adhesion, protein folding, chromatin remodelling and zinc sensing, to name but a few [[cite:PUB00035812]]. Zinc-binding motifs are stable structures, and they rarely undergo conformational changes upon binding their target.

Name: TRAF2, second zinc finger
ShortDescription: TRAF2 regulates activation of NF-kappa-B and JNK and plays a central role in the regulation of cell survival and apoptosis [[cite:PUB00058618], [cite:PUB00062992]]. It has E3-ubiquitin protein ligase activity and promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of target proteins. It consists of an N-terminal domain with RING ([interpro:IPR018957]) and several zinc fingers, and a C-terminal TRAF domain that comprises a coiled-coil ([interpro:IPR032070]) and a TRAF-C domain [[cite:PUB00058618]]. This entry represents the second β-β-α zinc finger.

Name: TNF receptor-associated factor 2, MATH domain
ShortDescription:
TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) regulates activation of NF-kappa-B and JNK and plays a central role in the regulation of cell survival and apoptosis [[cite:PUB00062991], [cite:PUB00062992]].

TRAF2 is heavily regulated by ubiquitin signals. It has E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase activity and promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of target proteins. Alternatively, TRAF2 may be required for recruiting other E3 ligases, such as A20, to help processing and turnover. Furthermore, TRAF2 is regulated by both K63 and K48 type ubiquitin chains. K63 linkage may be mediated by TRAF2 auto-ubiquitination, and is required for TRAF2 activation. c-IAPl and Siah2 are known E3 ligases that can K48-ubiquitinate TRAF2 to target it for proteasome-dependent degradation [[cite:PUB00062996], [cite:PUB00062993], [cite:PUB00018489]]. TRAF2 contains a RING finger domain, five zinc finger domains, and a TRAF domain.

;

The TRAF domain can be divided into a more divergent N-terminal α helical region (TRAF-N), and a highly conserved C-terminal MATH subdomain (TRAF-C) with an eight-stranded β-sandwich structure. TRAF-N mediates trimerization while TRAF-C interacts with receptors [[cite:PUB00011816], [cite:PUB00011815]].

Name: TNF receptor-associated factor 2, C3HC3D-type RING zinc finger
ShortDescription:
TNF receptor-associated factor 2 (TRAF2) regulates activation of NF-kappa-B and JNK and plays a central role in the regulation of cell survival and apoptosis [[cite:PUB00062991], [cite:PUB00062992]].

TRAF2 is heavily regulated by ubiquitin signals. It has E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase activity and promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of target proteins. Alternatively, TRAF2 may be required for recruiting other E3 ligases, such as A20, to help processing and turnover. Furthermore, TRAF2 is regulated by both K63 and K48 type ubiquitin chains. K63 linkage may be mediated by TRAF2 auto-ubiquitination, and is required for TRAF2 activation. c-IAPl and Siah2 are known E3 ligases that can K48-ubiquitinate TRAF2 to target it for proteasome-dependent degradation [[cite:PUB00062996], [cite:PUB00062993], [cite:PUB00018489]]. TRAF2 contains a RING finger domain, five zinc finger domains, and a TRAF domain.

;

This entry represents the modified C3HC3D-type (HC subclass) RING zinc finger of TRAF2 [[cite:PUB00058618]].

Name: Zinc finger, TRAF-type
ShortDescription:
This entry represents TRAF-type zinc finger domains. Some of the proteins that have this domain are mammalian signal transducers associated with the cytoplasmic domain of the 75kDa tumour necrosis factor receptor [[cite:PUB00015838]]. A heterocomplex, homodimer or heterodimer of TRAF1 and TRAF2, binds to the N-terminal of the inhibitor of apoptosis proteins 1 and 2 (IAPS) and recruits them to the tumour necrosis factor receptor 2. Other proteins containing this domain include F45G2.6 protein from Caenorhabditis elegans and DG17 protein from Dictyostelium discoideum (Slime mold).
