Name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthase small subunit, GATase1 domain
ShortDescription:
Glutamine amidotransferase (GATase) enzymes catalyse the removal of the ammonia group from glutamine and then transfer this group to a substrate to form a new carbon-nitrogen group [[cite:PUB00000003]]. The GATase domain exists either as a separate polypeptidic subunit or as part of a larger polypeptide fused in different ways to a synthase domain. Two classes of GATase domains have been identified [[cite:PUB00002062], [cite:PUB00002406]]: class-I (also known as trpG-type or triad) and class-II (also known as purF-type or Ntn). In class I glutamine amidotransferases, a triad of conserved Cys-His-Glu forms the active site, wherein the catalytic cysteine is essential for the amidotransferase activity [[cite:PUB00003933], [cite:PUB00043761]]. Different structures show that the active site Cys of type 1 GATase is located at the tip of a nucleophile elbow.

The E.coli carbamoyl phosphate synthase (CPSase) is a heterodimeric enzyme composed of a small and a large subunit (with the exception of CPSase III). CPSase catalyses the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from biocarbonate, ATP and glutamine or ammonia, and represents the first committed step in pyrimidine and arginine biosynthesis in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and in the urea cycle in most terrestrial vertebrates [[cite:PUB00006448], [cite:PUB00042597]]. The small subunit catalyses the hydrolysis of glutamine to ammonia, which in turn used by the large chain to synthesize carbamoyl phosphate. The C-terminal domain of the small subunit of CPSase has glutamine amidotransferase activity.

Name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthase, small subunit
ShortDescription: Carbamoyl phosphate synthase (CPSase) is a heterodimeric enzyme composed of a small and a large subunit (with the exception of CPSase III, see below). CPSase catalyses the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from biocarbonate, ATP and glutamine or ammonia, and represents the first committed step in pyrimidine and arginine biosynthesis in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and in the urea cycle in most terrestrial vertebrates [[cite:PUB00006448], [cite:PUB00042597]]. This entry represents the small subunit of the glutamine-dependent form ([ec:6.3.5.5]) of carbamoyl phosphate synthase. The small subunit catalyses the hydrolysis of glutamine to ammonia, which in turn used by the large chain to synthesize carbamoyl phosphate. The C-terminal domain of the small subunit of CPSase has glutamine amidotransferase activity.

Name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthase small subunit, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal domain of the small subunit of carbamoyl phosphate synthase. Structurally, it forms a 3-layer β/β/α fold of a type that is thought to be mobile in most proteins that carry it [[cite:PUB00023837], [cite:PUB00037058]].

Name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthase small subunit, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal domain superfamily of the small subunit of carbamoyl phosphate synthase. Structurally, it forms a 3-layer β/β/α fold of a type that is thought to be mobile in most proteins that carry it [[cite:PUB00023837], [cite:PUB00037058]].

Name: Dihydroorotase, catalytic domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the catalytic domain found in the family of bacterial dihydroorotases.

It also includes domains which are found in the multifunctional proteins r and pyr1-3 from Drosophila melanogaster and Dictyostelium discoideum, possessing dihydroorotase activity.

Name: Dihydroorotase, conserved site
ShortDescription:
This group contains a number of protein families, example are:

  • Archaeal and bacterial dihydroorotase ([ec:3.5.2.3]) (DHOase)
  • Allantoinase ([ec:3.5.2.5])

Dihydroorotase belongs to MEROPS peptidase family M38 (clan MJ), where it is classified as a non-peptidase homologue. DHOase catalyses the third step in thede novobiosynthesis of pyrimidine, the conversion of ureidosuccinic acid (N-carbamoyl-L-aspartate) into dihydroorotate. Dihydroorotase binds a zinc ion which is required for its catalytic activity [[cite:PUB00002652]].

In bacteria, DHOase is a dimer of identical chains of about 400 amino-acid residues (gene pyrC) [[cite:PUB00070199]]. In higher eukaryotes, DHOase is part of a large multi-functional protein known as 'rudimentary' in Drosophila melanogaster and CAD in mammals and which catalyzes the first three steps of pyrimidine biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00000720]]. The DHOase domain is located in the central part of this polyprotein. In yeasts, DHOase is encoded by a monofunctional protein (gene URA4). However, a defective DHOase domain [[cite:PUB00001777]] is found in a multifunctional protein (gene URA2) that catalyzes the first two steps of pyrimidine biosynthesis.

The comparison of DHOase sequences from various sources shows [[cite:PUB00003725]] that there are two highly conserved regions. The first located in the N-terminal extremity contains two histidine residues suggested [[cite:PUB00001777]] to be involved in binding the zinc ion. The second is found in the C-terminal part. Members of this family of proteins are predicted to adopt a TIM barrel fold [[cite:PUB00004994]].

Allantoinase ([ec:3.5.2.5]) is the enzyme that hydrolyzes allantoin into allantoate. In yeast (gene DAL1) [[cite:PUB00005645]], it is the first enzyme in the allantoin degradation pathway; in amphibians [[cite:PUB00002839]] and fishs it catalyzes the second step in the degradation of uric acid. The sequence of allantoinase is evolutionary related to that of DHOases.

Name: Bifunctional protein PyrR
ShortDescription: The PyrR protein from Bacillus subtilis and many other bacteria is a bifunctional protein. Its primary function is the regulation of expression of pyrimidine biosynthetic (pyr) genes by binding to specific sites on pyr mRNA in a uridine nucleotide-dependent manner and altering the folding of downstream RNA to promote termination of transcription. PyrR also catalyzes the uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (UPRTase) reaction ([ec:2.4.2.9]) even though it bears little amino acid sequence similarity to other bacterial UPRTases [[cite:PUB00053983]].

Name: PyrR bifunctional
ShortDescription: The PyrR bifunctional protein family is involved in the regulation of the pyrimidine nucleotide (pyr) operon. Members of this family bind to specific sites on pyr mRNA in a uridine-dependent manner, which influences the formation of RNA secondary structures. This binding disrupts an antiterminator hairpin and promotes the formation of a downstream transcription terminator, leading to decreased expression of downstream genes. Additionally, these proteins exhibit a weak uracil phosphoribosyltransferase activity, although this function is not considered physiologically significant. The primary role of the PyrR family is to modulate the transcription of the pyr operon in response to the presence of exogenous pyrimidines, ensuring proper regulation of pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis.

Name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthase large chain, methylglyoxal synthase-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the methylglyoxal synthase-like domain from type II glutamine-dependent carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CSP). CSP, a CarA and CarB heterodimer, catalyzes the production of carbamoyl phosphate which is subsequently employed in the metabolic pathways responsible for the synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides or arginine. The MGS-like domain is the C-terminal domain of CarB and appears to play a regulatory role in CPS function by binding allosteric effector molecules, including UMP and ornithine [[cite:PUB00042597]].

Name: Paramyxovirus structural protein P/V, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
The replicative complex of Paramyxoviridae consists of proteins N, P and L. Transcription and replication are carried out on the N/RNA template by a RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex, made of the phosphoprotein (P) and the large protein (L). P is organised into two moieties that are functionally and structurally distinct: a C-terminal moiety (PCT) and an N-terminal moiety (PNT). PCT is the most conserved in sequence and contains all regions required for virus transcription, whereas PNT, which is poorly conserved, provides several additional functions required for replication [[cite:PUB00045065]]. P protein plays a crucial role in the enzyme by positioning L onto the N/RNA template through an interaction with the C-terminal domain of N. Without P, L is not functional. The N-terminal part of P (PNT) is a chaperone for N and prevents it from binding to non-viral RNA in the infected cell [[cite:PUB00067736]].

This entry represents the PNT domain, found in several Paramyxoviridae (mainly Morbillivirus) structural protein P and V sequences [[cite:PUB00019995]]. V is a non-structural protein translated from an edited mRNA that contains an extra G residue.

Name: Paramyxovirinae protein V, zinc-binding domain
ShortDescription:
The paramyxoviruses, which include such respiroviruses as para-influenzae and measles, produce phosphoproteins - protein P - that are integral to the polymerase transcription-replication complex. Protein P consists of two functionally distinct moieties, an N-terminal PNT, and a C-terminal PCT [[cite:PUB00045065]].

The P mRNA encodes a variety of proteins beyond P. Protein V consists of PNT fused to a C-terminal zinc-binding region. This conserved region consists of the two-zinc-binding section sandwiched between β sheets 6 and 7 of the overall V protein. It is the binding of this core domain of V protein with the DDB1 protein (part of the ubiquitin-ligase complex) of eukaryotes which represents the key element of the virus-host protein interaction [[cite:PUB00039527]]. In the Henipavirus family, which includes Nipah and Hendra viruses, the V protein is able to block IFN (interferon) signalling by preventing IFN-induced STAT phosphorylation and nuclear translocation [[cite:PUB00055980]].

Name: BTN/MOG-like
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes Butyrophilin-like proteins, Myelin-oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, Selection and upkeep of intraepithelial T-cells protein 1 among others. This family of proteins is involved in various immune functions, including the modulation of T-cell-mediated responses, such as activation, proliferation, cytokine production, and development of cytotoxicity. Members of this family may act as costimulatory signals for T-cell and B-cell responses, influencing both adaptive and innate immune mechanisms. Some proteins within this family are implicated in cell-cell adhesion processes, particularly in the context of myelin sheath maintenance and cell communication. Additionally, they may play roles in the negative regulation of T-cell proliferation, and in the case of tumor macrophages, contribute to the suppression of tumor-associated antigen-specific T-cell immunity. Certain members are also involved in the secretion of milk-fat droplets and may act as receptors for the association of cytoplasmic droplets with the apical plasma membrane.

Name: Butyrophylin-like, SPRY domain
ShortDescription:
Several proteins that contain RING fingers also contain a well-conserved 40-residue cysteine-rich domain termed a B-box zinc finger. Often, one or two copies of the B-box are associated with a coiled coil domain ([interpro:IPR003649]) in addition to the ring finger ([interpro:IPR001841]), forming a tripartite motif. The tripartite motif is found in transcription factors, ribonucleoproteins and proto-oncoproteins, but no function has yet been ascribed to the domain [[cite:PUB00006153]].

The solution structure of the B-box motif has been determined by NMR. The protein is a monomer, with 2 β-strands, 2 helical turns and 3 extended loop regions packed in a novel topology [[cite:PUB00006018]]. Of 7 potential zinc ligands, only 4 are used, binding a single zinc atom in a C2-H2 tetrahedral arrangement. The B-box structure differs in tertiary fold from all other known zinc-binding motifs.

A group of proteins that contain the B-box motif also host a well conserved domain of unknown function. Proteins that include this domain are, e.g.: butyrophilin, the RET finger protein, the 52kDa Ro protein and the Xenopus nuclear factor protein. The C-terminal portion of this region has been termed the SPRY domain (after SPla and the RYanodine Receptor) [[cite:PUB00006153]].

Name: Concanavalin A-like lectin/glucanase domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents the concanavalin A-like domain, which has a sandwich structure of 12-14 β-strands in two sheets with a complex topology. Proteins containing this domain include:

  • Legume lectins
  • Glycosyl hydrolases family 16
  • Galectin (animal S-lectin)

  • Glycosyl hydrolase family 7
  • Xylanase/endoglucanase
  • Calnexin/calreticulin
  • Lectin leg-like
  • vp4 sialic acid binding protein
  • Trypanosoma sialidase
  • Thrombospondin
  • Hypothetical protein YesU
  • Alginate lyase
  • Glycosyl hydrolases family 32
  • Peptidase A4
  • Alpha-L-arabinofuranosidase B
  • SPRY domain containing proteins
  • Beta-D-xylosidase
  • SO2946-like
  • MAM domain containing proteins

Name: Butyrophilin subfamily 3 member A2-like, Ig-C domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in proteins from B7 family, including Butyrophilin subfamily 3 member A1/A2 (BTN3A1/A2) and similar proteins [[cite:PUB00154378], [cite:PUB00154379]]. BTN3A2 is a protein that plays a role in T-cell responses in the adaptive immune response [[cite:PUB00154378]]. BTN3A2 shows two extracellular domains: an N-terminal Ig-V like domain ([interpro:IPR013106]) and a C-terminal Ig-C type domain that is located in the centre of the protein sequence [[cite:PUB00153839]].

Name: SPRY-associated
ShortDescription:
PRY is a 50-60 amino acids domain associated with SPRY domains, adjacent to its N-terminal. The SPRY domain ([interpro:IPR003877]) is a protein-protein interaction module involved in many important signaling pathways [[cite:PUB00085899], [cite:PUB00041714]]. Distant homologues are domains in butyrophilin/marenostrin/pyrin, evolutionarily more ancient than SPRY/B30.2 counterpart. PRY and SPRY domains are structurally very similar and consist of a β sandwich fold [[cite:PUB00085899], [cite:PUB00041714]]. Ca2+-release from the sarcoplasmic or endoplasmic reticulum, the intracellular Ca2+ store, is mediated by the ryanodine receptor (RyR) and/or the inositol trisphosphate receptor (IP3R).

The proteins identified by the PRY domain, clearly fall into 3 sets which can be defined by their combination of signatures:

  • This group contains an immunoglobulin domain N-terminal to the PRY and butyrophilin domains. Butyrophilins are glycoproteins that are expressed on the apical surfaces of secretory cells in lactating mammary tissue and which may function in the secretion of milk-fat droplets.
  • This group contain a RING-finger domain N-terminal to the PRY domain. The RING-finger is a specialised type of Zn-finger of 40 to 60 residues that binds two atoms of zinc, and is probably involved in mediating protein-protein interactions. There are two different variants, the C3HC4-type and a C3H2C3-type, which is clearly related despite the different cysteine/histidine pattern. The latter type is sometimes referred to as 'RING-H2 finger' is not found associated with this group of proteins. This set of proteins are described as TRIM (TRIpartite Motif) family members and are involved in cellular compartmentalisation [[cite:PUB00009682]]. The TRIM family sequences are defined by a Ring finger domain, a B-box type1 (B1) and a B-box type 2 (B2) followed by a coiled-coil (CC) region [[cite:PUB00009683]]. Genes belonging to this family are implicated in a variety of processes such as development and cell growth and are involved in human disease.

Many of these proteins, with the PRY domain have a number of C-terminal signatures, SPRY, RFP-like (also known as B30.2 domain or PRYSPRY) and butyrophilin domain [[cite:PUB00009560]].

The third set of proteins have the C-terminal signatures but have no N-terminal RING-finger or immunoglobulin domain signatures. These proteins have not been functionally described.

Name: B30.2/SPRY domain
ShortDescription: The B30.2 domain was first identified as a protein domain encoded by an exon (named B30-2) in the Homo sapiens class I major histocompatibility complex region [[cite:PUB00033710]], whereas the SPRY domain was first identified in a Dictyostelium discoideum kinase splA and mammalian calcium-release channels ryanodine receptors [[cite:PUB00005467]]. B30.2 domain consists of PRY and SPRY subdomains. The SPRY domains (after SPla and the RYanodine Receptor) are shorter at the N terminus than the B30.2 domains. The ~200-residue B30.2/SPRY (for B30.2 and/or SPRY) domain is present in a large number of proteins with diverse individual functions in different biological processes. The B30.2/SPRY domain in these proteins is likely to function through protein-protein interaction [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The N-terminal ~60 residues of B30.2/SPRY domains are poorly conserved and, as a consequence, a new domain name PRY was coined for a group of similar sequence segments N-terminal to the SPRY domains [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The B30.2/SPRY domain contains three highly conserved motifs (LDP, WEVE and LDYE) [[cite:PUB00033712]]. The B30.2/SPRY domain adopts a highly distorted, compact β-sandwich fold with two additional short β-helices at the N terminus. The β-sandwich of the B30.2/SPRY domain consists of two layers of β-sheets: sheet A composed of eight strands and sheet B composed of seven strands. All the β-strands are in antiparallel arrangement [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The 5th β-strand corresponding to WEVE motif [[cite:PUB00033713]]. Both the N- and C-terminal ends of the B30.2/SPRY domains in general are close to each other [[cite:PUB00033711]].

Name: Butyrophilin subfamily 1/2, SPRY/PRY domain
ShortDescription: This domain, consisting of the distinct N-terminal PRY subdomain followed by the SPRY subdomain, is found at the C-terminal of butyrophilin family 1A and 2A (BTN1A and BTN2A). BTNs belong to receptor glycoproteins of immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily, characterised by the presence of extracellular Ig-like domains (IgV and/or IgC). BTN1A plays a role in the secretion, formation and stabilisation of milk fat globules. The B30.2 domain of BTN1A1 binds the enzyme xanthine oxidoreductase (XOR) in order to participate in milk fat globule secretion; this interaction may lead to the production of reactive oxygen species, which have immunomodulatory and antimicrobial functions [[cite:PUB00087938]]. Duplication events have led to three paralogues of BTN2A in primates: BTN2A1, BTN2A2, and BTN2A3 [[cite:PUB00087941]]. In humans, only BTN2A1 has been functionally characterised; it has been detected on epithelial cells and leukocytes, and identified as a novel ligand of dendritic cell-specific ICAM-3 grabbing nonintegrin (DCSIGN), a C-type lectin receptor that acts as an internalisation receptor for HIV-1, HCV, and other pathogens [[cite:PUB00087943]]. BTN2A2 mRNA is expressed in circulating human immune cells.

Name: SPRY domain
ShortDescription:
The SPRY domain is a ~140-amino-acid protein interaction module involved in many important signalling pathways like RNA processing, regulation of histone H3 methylation, innate immunity, or embryonic development [[cite:PUB00041714], [cite:PUB00085899], [cite:PUB00095661]]. It can be divided into 11 subfamilies based on amino acid sequence similarity or the presence of additional protein domains. Functionally, SPRY domains mediate critical interactions in diverse pathways: SSB-2 binds Par-4 to regulate apoptosis, RanBPM/SSB-1 interact with c-Met for signalling modulation, and SPSB proteins target iNOS for ubiquitination in immune regulation [[cite:PUB00039269], [cite:PUB00086126], [cite:PUB00130360]].

;

The B30.2 domain was first identified as a protein domain encoded by an exon (named B30-2) in the Homo sapiens class I major histocompatibility complex region [[cite:PUB00033710]], whereas the SPRY domain was first identified in a Dictyostelium discoideum kinase splA and mammalian calcium-release channels ryanodine receptors [[cite:PUB00005467]]. B30.2 domain consists of PRY and SPRY subdomains. The SPRY domains (after SPla and the RYanodine Receptor) are shorter at the N terminus than the B30.2 domains. The ~200-residue B30.2/SPRY (for B30.2 and/or SPRY) domain is present in a large number of proteins with diverse individual functions in different biological processes. The B30.2/SPRY domain in these proteins is likely to function through protein-protein interaction [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The N-terminal ~60 residues of B30.2/SPRY domains are poorly conserved and, as a consequence, a new domain name PRY was coined for a group of similar sequence segments N-terminal to the SPRY domains [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The B30.2/SPRY domain contains three highly conserved motifs (LDP, WEVE and LDYE) [[cite:PUB00033712]]. The B30.2/SPRY domain adopts a highly distorted, compact β-sandwich fold with two additional short β-helices at the N terminus. The β-sandwich of the B30.2/SPRY domain consists of two layers of β-sheets: sheet A composed of eight strands and sheet B composed of seven strands. All the β-strands are in antiparallel arrangement [[cite:PUB00033711]]. The 5th β-strand corresponding to WEVE motif [[cite:PUB00033713]]. Both the N- and C-terminal ends of the B30.2/SPRY domains in general are close to each other [[cite:PUB00033711]].

Name: B30.2/SPRY domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily also matches diverse E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases. This protein is involved in the apoptosis process [[cite:PUB00084879], [cite:PUB00093725]].

;
